## 1️⃣ What Is Software Testing?

**Software testing** is a **set of activities** carried out to discover defects and evaluate the quality of the work products produced during software development. While being tested, these work products are called **test objects**.

* 💥 **Software that does not work** → loss of money, time and business reputation; in extreme cases injury or death
* 🛡️ **Testing** → assesses quality and **reduces the risk of failure** in operation

---

## 2️⃣ Two Big Misconceptions About Testing

### ❌ Misconception 1 — "Testing is running the software and checking the results"
Test execution is only **one part** of testing. Planning, analysis, design, implementation and completion are testing too, and testing must be **aligned with the SDLC**.

### ❌ Misconception 2 — "Testing is only verification"
Testing covers **validation** as well as verification.

---

## 3️⃣ Verification vs Validation

| | **Verification** | **Validation** |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Does the system meet the specified requirements? | Does the system meet users' and stakeholders' needs? |
| **Measured against** | The written requirement | The real operational environment |
| **Example (hotel booking)** | Is the "10% discount for stays longer than 3 nights" rule coded correctly? | Can a customer actually complete a booking easily? |

> 🔑 **Verification** → "Did we build it right?", **Validation** → "Did we build the right thing?"

---

## 4️⃣ Static Testing vs Dynamic Testing

| | **Static Testing** | **Dynamic Testing** |
|---|---|---|
| **How?** | Without executing the code | By executing the code |
| **When?** | Early | After the code is written |
| **Finding defects** | Earlier and cheaper | Later and more expensive |
| **Example** | Reviews, static analysis, requirements inspection | Unit testing, system testing |

> 🔑 Static testing finds defects **earlier** and **more cheaply**

---

## 5️⃣ Testing Is Not Only a Technical Activity

* 📋 **It is managed** → planned, estimated, monitored and controlled (see chapter 5)
* 🧰 **Tools are used** → but the tool does not test, the tester does (see chapter 6)
* 🧠 **It is largely an intellectual activity** → it needs specialized knowledge, analytical skills, **critical thinking** and **systems thinking**
* 📘 Further reading: **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1**

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Concept | In short |
|---|---|
| **Software testing** | Set of activities to find defects and evaluate quality |
| **Test object** | The work product being tested (code, requirement, design...) |
| **Verification** | Does it match the specification? |
| **Validation** | Does it serve the user? |
| **Static testing** | Inspecting without running |
| **Dynamic testing** | Trying by running |

## 1️⃣ What Is a Test Objective?

Test objectives tell us **why we test**. These are the typical objectives listed by ISTQB.

---

## 2️⃣ Typical Test Objectives (ISTQB)

### ✅ These ARE test objectives:
* 🧐 **Evaluating work products** → requirements, user stories, designs, code
* 🐛 **Causing failures and finding defects**
* 🎯 **Ensuring the required coverage of a test object**
* ⚠️ **Reducing the risk level of inadequate software quality**
* 📋 **Verifying whether specified requirements have been fulfilled**
* ⚖️ **Verifying compliance with contractual, legal and regulatory requirements**
* 📊 **Providing information to stakeholders so they can make informed decisions** (e.g. the release decision)
* 💪 **Building confidence in the quality of the test object**
* 👤 **Validating that the test object is complete and works as stakeholders expect**

### ❌ These are NOT test objectives:
* Finding the root cause and fixing the defect → that is **debugging**
* Proving that no defects remain → **impossible!** (1st testing principle)
* Defining and improving quality processes → that is **QA**
* Fixing the code and shipping the release → that is the **developer's** job

---

## 3️⃣ Objectives Are Not Fixed

Test objectives **vary with context**:

| Context factor | Example impact |
|---|---|
| **Work product being tested** | A requirements document or the code? |
| **Test level** | Component testing leans to finding defects, acceptance testing to building confidence |
| **Risks** | ATM cash withdrawal → risk reduction; blog theme → confidence building |
| **SDLC** | Agile wants fast feedback, sequential models want thorough verification |
| **Business context** | Time to market, competition, corporate structure |

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What does testing do?** | Evaluates, finds defects, ensures coverage, reduces risk |
| **Who does testing serve?** | The stakeholders who must decide |
| **What can testing prove?** | That defects **are present** — never that they are **absent** |
| **Are objectives fixed?** | No, they depend on the context |

## 1️⃣ Testing or Debugging?

These are **separate activities**, and usually **different people** do them.

| Concept | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Testing** | Triggering a failure or finding a defect directly | 50 TL was loaded onto the card, only 5 TL appeared → report it |
| **Defect** | The error as it appears in the code | The wrong multiplier in the code |
| **Failure** | The defect showing up during execution | The balance displayed incorrectly |
| **Debugging** | Finding the cause of the failure and removing it | Inspecting the code and fixing the wrong line |

> 🔑 **Testing** → finds, **Debugging** → fixes

---

## 2️⃣ The 3 Steps of Debugging (after dynamic testing)

```
1. Reproduction of the failure
       ↓
2. Diagnosis (finding the defect)
       ↓
3. Fixing the defect
```

All three steps are **debugging**, not testing. Debugging is typically the **developer's** job.

---

## 3️⃣ What Happens After the Fix?

* ✅ **Confirmation testing** → Did the fix really resolve the problem? Preferably run by the **same person who ran the initial test**.
* 🔁 **Regression testing** → Did the fix break something else?

> Both of these are **testing** again, not debugging.

---

## 4️⃣ After Static Testing, Debugging Is Shorter

* 📖 Static testing does not execute the code → **no failure occurs**, the defect is found **directly**
* ⚡ So **reproduction and diagnosis are not needed**
* 🔧 Only **removing the defect** is left

---

## 🧠 Summary Chain

```
Test executed → failure observed        (TESTING)
    ↓
Failure reproduced                      (DEBUGGING)
    ↓
Defect diagnosed                        (DEBUGGING)
    ↓
Code fixed                              (DEBUGGING)
    ↓
Confirmation + regression testing       (TESTING)
```

> 🔑 In the exam: if it says "find the cause, analyze it, fix it" → **debugging**. If it says "execute, compare, report" → **testing**.

## 1️⃣ What Does Testing Bring to a Project?

* 💰 **It is a cost-effective way of detecting defects** → the defects found are then removed (by **debugging**, a non-testing activity), so testing contributes **indirectly** to a higher quality product
* 📊 **It measures quality directly** → the quality of the test object is evaluated at various phases of the SDLC
* 🚦 **It feeds decisions** → these measures are used in project management; moving to the next phase and the **release decision** rest on them
* 👤 **It represents users indirectly** → testers make sure user needs are considered throughout the SDLC; involving a real user group is usually **too expensive or not possible**
* ⚖️ **It meets legal and contractual obligations** → testing may be required to comply with regulatory standards

---

## 2️⃣ Careful: Testing Finds, It Does Not Fix

| Activity | What it does | Who does it |
|---|---|---|
| **Testing** | Finds and reports the defect/failure | Tester (and other stakeholders) |
| **Debugging** | Removes the defect | Developer |

> 🔑 Testing does not raise quality **directly**; it raises it **indirectly** by making defects visible

---

## 3️⃣ Concrete Example — Airline Seat Selection

> **Scenario:** Before coding starts, the requirements document goes through a review that testers take part in.

```
Finding: "What happens if the same seat is assigned to two passengers?" is specified nowhere
    ↓
This gap in the requirement was found BEFORE any code was written
    ↓
Cost to fix: a few hours
    ↓
If found in production: double bookings, complaints, reputation damage 💸
```

* ✅ This is an example of testing contributing to success **early** (through static testing)
* ✅ In the same way, testers joining **requirements workshops** and **user story refinement sessions** expose ambiguous acceptance criteria before a line of code exists

---

| 🚦 **Decision** | Feeds the release decision |
| 👤 **Representation** | Represents the user in the project |
| ⚖️ **Compliance** | Meets legal and contractual requirements |

## 1️⃣ Testing vs Quality Assurance (QA)

People use these two terms interchangeably, but they are **not the same**.

| | **Testing** | **Quality Assurance (QA)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | Product | Process |
| **Approach** | Corrective | Preventive |
| **Question** | Is the product right? | Is the process right? |
| **Who?** | Test team (and stakeholders) | **Everyone** on the project |
| **Example** | Was the story deleted after 24 hours? | Why do we keep producing timer defects? |

> 🔑 **Testing** puts out the fire, **QA** prevents the fire from starting

---

## 2️⃣ Testing = One Form of Quality Control (QC)

Testing is the **major form of quality control** — but not the only one.

### ✅ Other quality control methods:
* 📐 **Formal methods** → model checking, proof of correctness
* 🧪 **Simulation**
* 🧱 **Prototyping**

---

## 3️⃣ How Does QA Work?

* 🔄 It focuses on the **implementation and improvement of processes**
* 💡 Its core assumption: **"If a good process is followed correctly, it will generate a good product"**
* 🌍 It applies to both the **development** and the **testing** process
* 👥 It is **everyone's responsibility** on the project — not the monopoly of a separate "QA department"

---

## 4️⃣ The Same Test Results, Two Different Uses

```
Test results
    ├── On the TESTING side → used to fix defects
    └── On the QA side      → provide feedback on how well the development
                              and test processes are performing
```

> 💡 Example: An e-commerce cart produced the same kind of discount calculation defect in three releases in a row.
> **Testing:** finds and reports all three defects.
> **QA:** changes the **process** — "pricing rules must be reviewed with the business analyst before they are coded".

---

| Concept | Focus | Nature | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quality Assurance (QA)** | Process | Preventive | Everyone |
| **Quality Control (QC)** | Product | Corrective | Those checking the product |
| **Testing** | Product | The major form of QC | Test team + stakeholders |

## 1️⃣ Core Definitions

| Concept | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Root Cause** | The **fundamental reason** a problem occurred (person, process, environment) |
| **Error (Mistake)** | A **wrong action or decision made by a human** |
| **Defect (Fault / Bug)** | The error **as it ends up in the code or a document** |
| **Failure** | The defective code **behaving wrongly when executed** |

> 🔑 The chain: **Root Cause → Error → Defect → Failure**

---

## 2️⃣ 👤 Why Do People Make Errors?

* ⏰ **Time pressure** → rushing
* 🧩 **Complex work products** → hard requirements, complicated code
* 😴 **Tiredness** → loss of attention
* 📚 **Inadequate training** → not really knowing the subject
* 🗣️ **Poor interaction** → misunderstandings
* 🏗️ **Weak process or infrastructure** → an environment that makes work harder

---

## 3️⃣ 📍 Where Are Defects Found?

* 📋 **In requirements documents** → a wrong or missing requirement
* 💻 **In source code** → a wrongly written line
* 🧪 **In test scripts** → a faulty test case
* 📦 **In build or configuration files** → wrong settings

---

## 4️⃣ 🔁 How Do Defects Spread?

* A defect introduced early in the SDLC that is **not detected** →
* leads to **defective work products** in later phases →
* and gets **bigger and more expensive** 💸

> Example: The requirement was wrong → the code was wrong → the test was wrong → a faulty product reached the user

---

## 5️⃣ ⚡ Not Every Defect Always Causes a Failure!

* 🔴 **Defects that always cause a failure** → the system breaks every time the code runs
* 🟡 **Defects that sometimes cause a failure** → only under specific circumstances
* 🟢 **Defects that never cause a failure** → they sit in the code but are never triggered

> Example: Code that only runs on 29 February → a failure once every four years!

---

## 6️⃣ 🌍 Errors Are Not the Only Cause of Failures

* ☢️ **Radiation** → can cause defects in firmware
* 📡 **Electromagnetic fields** → can disturb the system
* 🌡️ **Environmental conditions** → extreme heat, humidity, etc.

> So a failure can happen even when nobody made an error!

---

## 7️⃣ 🔍 What Is a Root Cause?

* It is the **fundamental reason** a problem occurred (e.g. a situation that leads to an error)
* **Root cause analysis** is performed when a failure occurs or a defect is identified
* **Removing the root cause** prevents similar failures/defects or reduces how often they happen

```
Failure: The application crashed
Defect: The code was written incorrectly
Root Cause: The developer had no training
Fix: Provide training → similar defects stop appearing
```

---

## 📌 Example 1 — Bonus Calculation & Users with Disabilities

### Scenario:
* A **tired** designer produced a UI design that did not consider users with disabilities
* A programmer **under time pressure** left out exception handling for bonus calculations
* Users with disabilities complained → the company was **fined**
* The occasionally wrong bonus calculation went unnoticed

### Classification:
| Concept | In this example |
|---|---|
| **Root Cause** | The programmer working **under time pressure** ✅ |
| **Error** | The designer's **decision to ignore users with disabilities** |
| **Defect** | Bonuses **sometimes calculated wrongly** (in the code, never triggered) |
| **Failure** | The company **receiving a fine** (the system behaved wrongly) |

> ❌ The fine is a **consequence of a failure**, not the failure itself
> ❌ The untriggered bonus problem sitting in the code is a **defect**, not a failure

---

## 📌 Example 2 — Online Exam Proctoring System

### Scenario:
* The session should close when the exam time runs out, but it **stayed open**
* The developer used the **wrong operator** in the time comparison
* The team had received **no training** on handling time units

### Classification:
| Concept | In this example |
|---|---|
| **Root Cause** | The team being given **no training** ✅ |
| **Error** | The developer **typing the wrong operator** |
| **Defect** | The **wrong operator in the code** |
| **Failure** | The **session staying open** |

```
No training (Root Cause)
    ↓
Developer wrote the wrong operator (Error)
    ↓
The wrong operator stayed in the code (Defect)
    ↓
The session did not close (Failure)
```

---

## 📌 Example 3 — Hotel Pricing Engine

### Scenario:
* The discount must apply **ONLY to stays LONGER than 3 nights**
* The developer misunderstood the rule → coded it as **"3 nights or more"**
* A 3-night booking wrongly received the discount

### Classification:
| Concept | In this example |
|---|---|
| **Error** | The developer **misunderstanding the rule** ✅ |
| **Defect** | The **wrong condition in the code** — `>=3` where it should be `>3` ✅ |
| **Failure** | The **discount wrongly applied** to a 3-night booking ✅ |

```
Misunderstood the rule (Error)
    ↓
Wrote the wrong condition in code (Defect)
    ↓
Customer got the wrong discount (Failure)
```

---

## 🧠 Everything in One Table

| Concept | Definition | Example 1 | Example 2 | Example 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Root Cause** | Fundamental reason | Time pressure | No training given | — |
| **Error** | Human's wrong action | Skipping accessibility in the UI | Typing the wrong operator | Misunderstanding the rule |
| **Defect** | The error in the code | Bonus calculation defect | Wrong operator in the code | Wrong condition in the code |
| **Failure** | System behaving wrongly | Receiving a fine | Session staying open | Wrong discount applied |

---

## 🔑 Golden Rule

```
Root Cause → "Why was the mistake made?"  → No training, tiredness, pressure
Error      → "What did the human do?"     → Misunderstood it, typed it wrong
Defect     → "What is in the code?"       → Wrong operator, wrong condition
Failure    → "What did the system do?"    → Crashed, gave a wrong result
```

## 1️⃣ Testing Shows the Presence, Not the Absence of Defects

* Testing lets you say **"defects are present"** ✅
* It never lets you say **"there are no defects"** ❌
* Testing only **reduces the probability of undiscovered defects remaining**
* Even if every test passes, the software may still fail to meet users' needs

> 💡 Example: You tested a hotel booking site and found nothing → that does not mean "the site is perfect", only "you did not find anything"

---

## 2️⃣ Exhaustive Testing Is Impossible

* Testing everything burns **all your time and money** (it is infeasible except in trivial cases)
* Use these instead:
  * 🎯 **Risk-based testing** → test the riskiest areas first (see section 5.2)
  * 📋 **Test case prioritization** → run the important tests first (see section 5.1.5)
  * 🔧 **Test techniques** → test smartly (see chapter 4)

> 💡 Example: In an e-commerce cart the **payment flow** matters far more than the dark mode color → test that first

---

## 3️⃣ Early Testing Saves Time and Money

* The **earlier** a defect is found, the **cheaper** it is to fix
* A defect removed early does not spawn new defects in **derived work products**
* That means fewer failures later in the SDLC → **lower cost of quality**
* Both **static** and **dynamic** testing should start as early as possible

```
Defect found at requirements stage → fixed in an hour
Defect found after go-live → takes weeks, costs customers 💸
```

---

## 4️⃣ Defects Cluster Together (Pareto)

* **Most** of the defects found sit in a **small number of components**
* The same few components also cause most of the operational failures
* This phenomenon illustrates the **Pareto principle**
* **Predicted** and **observed** defect clusters are an important input to **risk-based testing**

> 💡 Example: On an e-commerce site the payment and promotions modules produce far more defects than changing a profile picture → focus there

---

## 5️⃣ Tests Wear Out

* Repeating the same tests many times makes them **increasingly ineffective** at finding new defects
* The fix: **modify existing tests and test data, and write new tests**
* ⚠️ Exception: in some cases repeating the same tests is beneficial — e.g. **automated regression testing**

```
You always test with the same user, the same amount, the same browser
→ Try a different user, a different amount, a different device!
```

---

## 6️⃣ Testing Is Context Dependent

* There is **no single universally applicable approach** to testing
* A banking app ≠ a game ≠ a hospital system
* Testing differs with the project's type, risk and budget

```
Hospital software → very strict, thorough testing (lives at stake!)
A simple note-taking app → lighter testing is enough
```

---

## 7️⃣ Absence-of-Defects Fallacy

* Testing all specified requirements thoroughly + fixing every defect found → **can still produce bad software!**
* Because the software may:
  * Fail to meet users' needs and expectations
  * Fail to help the customer reach their business goals
  * Be inferior to competing products
* **Validation** must be carried out alongside verification

```
The app meets every specified requirement ✅
But users find it hard to use 😤
→ The tests passed, the software failed!
```

---

## 🧠 The 7 Principles in One Table

| # | Principle | In short |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Presence, not absence of defects | You can never say "no defects" |
| 2 | Exhaustive testing is impossible | Test smartly, by priority |
| 3 | Early testing saves money | Find early, fix cheaply |
| 4 | Defects cluster together | Few components, most defects |
| 5 | Tests wear out | The same test stops working |
| 6 | Testing is context dependent | Every project needs its own testing |
| 7 | Absence-of-defects fallacy | Tests can pass and the software still fail |

> 🔑 Exam tip: "The regression suite has not changed for months and finds nothing new" → **principle 5 (tests wear out)**. "We cannot test everything, let us prioritize" → **principle 2**.

## 🔄 General Note

> Although the activities look sequential, they are usually carried out **iteratively or in parallel**.
> They must be **tailored** to each system and project.

---

## 1️⃣ Test Planning
**"What will we do, and how?"**

* Test objectives are defined
* The **approach** that best achieves them within the constraints of the context is selected
* Resources, time and budget are planned (see section 5.1)

> 💡 **Example — an e-commerce cart feature:**
> - What gets tested? → Add to cart, change quantity, apply coupon
> - Who tests? → A team of 3 testers
> - When? → 2 weeks
> - Automated or manual? → Critical flows automated

---

## 2️⃣ Test Monitoring and Test Control
**"Is everything going according to plan?"**

* **Monitoring** → all test activities are checked continuously, actual progress is compared against the plan
* **Control** → the **actions** needed to meet the test objectives are taken (see section 5.3)

> 💡 **Example:**
> - Plan: 50 test cases per week
> - Actual: only 30 were run → **monitoring**
> - Action: the test environment went down → it was fixed, the schedule was updated → **control**

---

## 3️⃣ Test Analysis
**"WHAT should we test?"**

* The **test basis** is analyzed → testable features are identified
* **Test conditions** are defined and **prioritized**, taking risks and risk levels into account
* The test basis and the test object are evaluated for the defects they may contain and for **testability**
* The output is expressed in terms of **measurable coverage criteria**

> 💡 **Example — hotel booking:**
> - Requirement: "10% discount for stays longer than 3 nights"
> - Test conditions:
>   - Is the discount withheld for a 2-night booking?
>   - Is the discount withheld for a 3-night booking?
>   - Is the discount applied for a 4-night booking?

---

## 4️⃣ Test Design
**"HOW should we test it?"**

* Test conditions → elaborated into **test cases** and other testware (e.g. test charters)
* **Coverage items** are identified → they guide the choice of test case inputs
* **Test data requirements**, the **test environment design**, and the needed infrastructure and tools are defined
* Test techniques (boundary value analysis, equivalence partitioning, etc.) are applied here

> 💡 **Example — the discount case:**
> ```
> Case: A 3-night booking must NOT receive the discount
> Input: Check-in 01 June, check-out 04 June (3 nights)
> Expected result: No discount, full price ✅
> ```

---

## 5️⃣ Test Implementation
**"Are the tests ready to run?"**

* The **testware needed for execution is created or acquired** (e.g. test data)
* Test cases → organized into **test procedures**, assembled into **test suites**
* Manual and automated **test scripts** are written
* The **test execution schedule** is prepared and procedures are prioritized
* The **test environment is built** and verified to be set up correctly

> 💡 **Example:**
> - An automated test script was written with Selenium
> - The test database was prepared (dummy bookings created)
> - The environment was checked → "environment ready" sign-off obtained
> - Critical tests queued first, the rest after

---

## 6️⃣ Test Execution
**"What are the results?"**

* Tests are run **according to the execution schedule** (manually or automatically)
* Actual results → compared with expected results
* Results are **logged**
* **Anomalies** are analyzed to identify their likely causes and reported based on the failures observed (see section 5.5)

> 💡 **Example:**
> - The 3-night booking test was run
> - Expected: no discount
> - Actual: 10% discount applied ❌
> - A defect report was raised → sent to the developer

---

## 7️⃣ Test Completion
**"What did we learn, what do we archive?"**

* Usually happens at project milestones (release, end of iteration, test level completion)
* **Change requests** or **product backlog items** are created for unresolved defects
* Testware that may be useful later is **archived or handed over**
* The **test environment** is shut down to an agreed state
* **Lessons learned** are analyzed → improvements identified
* A **test completion report** is written and communicated to stakeholders

> 💡 **Example:**
> - 120 tests run in this release, 8 defects found, 7 fixed
> - 1 defect deferred to the next release → change request raised
> - Lesson learned: "Features with pricing rules need more testing"

---

| **Monitoring/Control** | Is the plan on track? | Weekly progress report |
| **Analysis** | WHAT to test? | List of test conditions |

## 📌 The Core Idea

> Testing is **not performed in isolation!**
> Test activities are an **integral part** of the development processes carried out within an organization.
> Testing is **funded by stakeholders**, and its final goal is to help fulfill their **business needs**.

---

## 🤔 The 8 Contextual Factors That Shape Testing

### 👥 1. Stakeholders
Needs, expectations, requirements, willingness to cooperate
> 💡 If the customer says "only test the payment screen" → the scope narrows

### 👨‍💻 2. Team Members
Skills, knowledge, level of experience, availability, training needs
> 💡 Nobody on the team knows automation → testing stays manual

### 🏢 3. Business Domain
Criticality of the test object, identified risks, market needs, legal regulations
> 💡 A public transport card top-up machine (money + audits) → formal documentation, wide coverage
> 💡 An internal-only reporting tool → much lighter testing

### 💻 4. Technical Factors
Type of software, product architecture, technology used
> 💡 A mobile app → testing across devices; a web app → testing across browsers

### ⏰ 5. Project Constraints
Scope, time, budget, resources
> 💡 One week left → only critical features get tested

### 🏗️ 6. Organizational Factors
Organizational structure, existing policies, practices used
> 💡 A policy of "regression is mandatory on every code change" → automation becomes a must

### 🔄 7. Software Development Lifecycle
Engineering practices, development methods
> 💡 Agile → testing at the end of every iteration; sequential models → testing after development ends

### 🔧 8. Tools
Availability, usability, compliance
> 💡 No automation tool or licence → manual testing

## 1️⃣ What Is Traceability?

**Traceability** means keeping the test basis elements and everything derived from them **linked** to each other.

```
Test basis (requirement, user story, risk)
    ↓
Test conditions
    ↓
Test cases
    ↓
Test results
    ↓
Defects
```

> 🔑 **Traceability** → being able to trace every defect back to a requirement, and every requirement forward to a result

---

## 2️⃣ Why Does It Matter?

* 📏 **Coverage evaluation** → if **measurable coverage criteria** are defined in the test basis, how much has been achieved can be measured
* 🎯 Coverage criteria act as **key performance indicators** showing to what extent the test objectives have been met
* 🔁 **Impact analysis** → when a requirement changes, the tests that must be updated are found instantly
* 🏛️ **Audits and IT governance** → you can show a regulator "this requirement was proven by these tests with these results"
* 📊 **Reporting** → progress and completion reports become clearer because they include the status of test basis elements
* 🗣️ **Communication** → the technical side of testing can be explained to stakeholders in understandable terms
* 📈 **Assessment** → product quality, process capability and project progress can be judged against business goals

---

## 3️⃣ Two Classic Examples (ISTQB)

| Traceability | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Test cases → requirements** | Verifying that the requirements are **covered by test cases** |
| **Test results → risks** | Evaluating the level of **residual risk** in the test object |

---

## 4️⃣ Concrete Example — Telehealth Consultation Platform

> **Situation:** Before each release the regulator wants to see which requirement was proven by which tests and with which results. The team must also find quickly which tests to update when a requirement changes.

```
Requirement R-14 "No consultation starts before patient identity is verified"
    ↓ traceability
Test conditions TC-7, TC-8
    ↓
Test cases TS-21, TS-22, TS-23  → 2 PASSED, 1 FAILED
    ↓
Defect DEF-105 (open)
```

* ✅ **Audit:** "R-14 has been tested, 1 defect is still open" → the evidence is ready
* ✅ **Impact analysis:** if R-14 changes → TS-21, TS-22, TS-23 must be updated, visible immediately
* ✅ **Residual risk:** the open defect keeps the risk on R-14 high → the release decision follows from that

---

## 1️⃣ The Two Roles in the Syllabus

ISTQB defines two principal roles: the **test management role** and the **testing role**. The tasks assigned to them depend on the **project and product context**, the people's **skills**, and the **organization**.

## 2️⃣ The Two Roles Compared

| **Responsibility** | The test process, the test team, **leadership** of test activities | The **engineering (technical)** side of testing |

| **Typical output** | Test plan, progress report, completion report | Test conditions, test cases, scripts, defect reports |
| **Question** | When, with whom, on what budget? | What and how will we test? |

Test execution             → TESTING

```

> 💡 Memory hook: the **first two and the last** activity sit with management, the **middle four** with the testing role.

## 1️⃣ The 6 Generic Skills a Tester Needs

| 🧪 **Testing knowledge** | Increases the **effectiveness** of testing | Catching the 3/4-night boundary with boundary value analysis |
| 🔍 **Thoroughness, carefulness, curiosity, attention to detail, being methodical** | Finding defects, especially the **hard-to-find** ones | Noticing a one-cent deviation in rounding |
| 🗣️ **Good communication, active listening, being a team player** | Interacting with all stakeholders, reporting and discussing defects | Writing a defect report that is objective, not accusatory |

## 2️⃣ ⚠️ The Tester Is the Bearer of Bad News

* 📨 Testers are often the ones **delivering bad news**
* 😠 **Blaming the bearer of bad news** is a common human trait
* 🎯 That is why **communication skills are crucial** for testers

---

## 3️⃣ Why Does Friction Appear?

* 🪞 Test results may be perceived as **criticism of the product and of its author**
* 🧲 **Confirmation bias** → people struggle to accept information that disagrees with what they already believe
* 💥 Some people see testing as a **destructive activity** — even though it contributes greatly to project success and product quality

---

## 4️⃣ ✅ The Fix: Constructive Communication

```
❌ "You wrecked the payment module again"
✅ "A 3-night booking receives the discount; requirement R-14 says 'longer than 3 nights'.
    Steps and a screenshot are attached."
```

* 🎯 Focus on the **finding**, not the person
* 📎 Give **evidence**: steps, expected vs actual, screenshot
* 👂 **Listen actively** → hear the developer's explanation too

## 1️⃣ What Is the Whole Team Approach?

One of the most important skills for a tester is **working effectively within a team** and contributing positively to the team's goals. The **whole team approach** builds on that skill and comes from **Extreme Programming (XP)** (see section 2.1).

* 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 **Any team member with the necessary knowledge and skills can perform any task**
* ✅ **Everyone is responsible for quality** — not only the test team
* 🏠 Team members share the **same workspace** (physical or virtual), because co-location facilitates communication and interaction

---

## 2️⃣ Benefits

| Benefit | What it means |
|---|---|
| 🤝 **Better team dynamics** | Relationships within the team improve |
| 🗣️ **More communication and collaboration** | Information travels fast inside the team |
| ⚡ **Synergy** | The team's various skill sets are leveraged for the project |
| 📚 **Knowledge transfer** | Testers pass testing knowledge to others and influence the product's development |

---

## 3️⃣ Who Does the Tester Work With?

```
Tester
   ├── With business representatives → helps them create suitable ACCEPTANCE TESTS
   └── With developers               → agrees the TEST STRATEGY and TEST AUTOMATION approach
```

> 💡 **Example — online auction platform:** During a user story refinement session the tester asks the business representative "What happens if a bid arrives in the closing second?" → the acceptance criterion is settled before any code is written.

---

## 4️⃣ ⚠️ It Is Not Always Appropriate

* 🚦 Depending on the context, the whole team approach **may not always fit**
* 🏥 For instance, **safety-critical** situations may require a **high level of test independence**

---

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Where does it come from?** | Extreme Programming (XP) |
| **Core principle?** | Anyone with the right skills can do any task |
| **Whose job is quality?** | Everyone's |
| **Why a shared workspace?** | It facilitates communication and interaction |
| **When does it not fit?** | Safety-critical situations needing high independence |

## 1️⃣ Why Does Independence Help?

* 🧠 The author's and the tester's **cognitive biases differ** → an independent tester is **more effective** at finding defects
* ⚠️ But **independence is not a replacement for familiarity** → developers can **efficiently** find many defects in their own code

> 🔑 **Independence** → brings a fresh pair of eyes, **Familiarity** → goes deep. They complement each other, they are not alternatives.

---

## 2️⃣ The 4 Levels of Independence

| Who tests | Independence |
|---|---|
| **The author themselves** | None |
| **Peers from the same team** | Some |
| **Testers outside the author's team but inside the organization** | High |
| **Testers outside the organization** | Very high |

> 💡 For most projects it is best to test at **multiple levels of independence**:
> ```
> Component + component integration testing → DEVELOPERS
> System + system integration testing       → TEST TEAM
> Acceptance testing                        → BUSINESS REPRESENTATIVES
> ```

---

## 3️⃣ ✅ Benefits

* 👁️ Different **backgrounds, technical perspectives and biases** → independent testers recognize **different kinds of failures and defects** than developers do
* ❓ An independent tester can **verify, challenge or disprove the assumptions** stakeholders made during specification and implementation

---

## 4️⃣ ❌ Drawbacks

* 🚧 Independent testers may become **isolated** from the development team → **lack of collaboration**, **communication problems**, even an **adversarial relationship**
* 🤷 Developers may **lose their sense of responsibility for quality** ("quality is the test team's job")
* ⏳ Independent testers may be seen as a **bottleneck** or **blamed for delays in release**

---

## 5️⃣ Concrete Example — Online Banking App

> **Situation:** Until now developers tested their own code. The team decides to hand all testing over to an independent test company **outside the organization**.

| Expected | Most likely drawback |
|---|---|
| ✅ Different kinds of defects will surface | ❌ Developers shed their responsibility for quality |
| ✅ Assumptions get challenged | ❌ Communication breaks down, the external team is seen as a bottleneck |

## 1️⃣ What Is an SDLC?

A **Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) model** is an **abstract, high-level map** of how software gets built.

An SDLC model says:

* 🧩 Which **development phases** and **types of activity** exist?
* 🔗 How are they related **logically**?
* ⏰ In what **chronological** order do they run?

> 🔑 An SDLC is a **framework** — the answer to "when do we do what". It is not a detailed recipe.

---

## 2️⃣ Three Families of SDLC Models

| Family | Logic | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequential** | Phases run one after another; the next starts when the previous ends | Waterfall, **V-model** |
| **Iterative** | The same work is reworked and refined round after round | Spiral model, **prototyping** |
| **Incremental** | The product grows in working slices | **Unified Process** |

> 💡 Example: build a hotel booking site with waterfall and you write every requirement first, then all the code. Build it incrementally and "room search" ships first, then "booking", then "payment".

---

## 3️⃣ Methods and Agile Practices

Activities **inside** an SDLC can be described by more detailed methods:

| Acronym | Stands for |
|---|---|
| **ATDD** | Acceptance Test-Driven Development |
| **BDD** | Behavior-Driven Development |
| **DDD** | Domain-Driven Design |
| **XP** | Extreme Programming |
| **FDD** | Feature-Driven Development |
| **TDD** | Test-Driven Development |
| **Kanban / Scrum / Lean IT** | Agile ways of working |

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is an SDLC model? | An abstract, high-level representation of the development process |
| What does it show? | The logical + chronological relation of phases |
| How many families? | 3 → sequential, iterative, incremental |
| Which family is the V-model? | **Sequential** |
| What are Scrum / TDD? | Not SDLC models → **methods / Agile practices** |

## 1️⃣ The Golden Rule

> Testing **must be adapted to the SDLC.** You cannot staple the same test approach onto every model.

---

## 2️⃣ What Does the Choice of SDLC Impact? (5 Items — Memorize)

| # | What is affected | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 🎯 **Scope and timing** of test activities (test levels, test types) | When can dynamic testing start? |
| 2 | 📄 **Level of detail** of test documentation | A 40-page test plan or a single page? |
| 3 | 🔧 Choice of **test techniques and approach** | Experience-based or design-based? |
| 4 | 🤖 **Extent of test automation** | Is regression fully automated? |
| 5 | 👤 **Role and responsibilities** of the tester | Does the tester join requirement reviews? |

---

## 3️⃣ Sequential vs Iterative/Incremental — The Exam's Favourite

| | **Sequential (waterfall, V-model)** | **Iterative / incremental** |
|---|---|---|
| **What testers do early** | Requirement reviews, test analysis, test design | The same **plus there is executable code** |
| **Early dynamic testing?** | ❌ Not possible — executable code comes later | ✅ Possible |
| **What each iteration delivers** | — | A working **prototype** or **product increment** |
| **Which test levels run** | One phase at a time | **All test levels in every iteration** |
| **Static + dynamic testing** | Static early, dynamic late | **Both, in every iteration** |
| **Regression need** | Low | 🔴 **Very high** (frequent delivery) |
| **Feedback** | Slow | ⚡ **Has to be fast** |

> 🔑 **Sequential** → dynamic testing starts late. **Iterative/incremental** → static *and* dynamic testing in every iteration, **at all test levels**.

---

## 4️⃣ What Changes in Agile Projects?

Agile assumes **change can happen throughout the project**. So:

* 📄 **Lightweight work product documentation** → no thick specs
* 🤖 **Extensive test automation** → to make regression testing easy
* 🧭 Most manual testing uses **experience-based techniques** (e.g. exploratory) → no extensive prior test analysis and design

---

## ❌ Common Trap

> "We moved from sequential to incremental, so now we test **less**" ❌
> Reality: **more often, faster, more automated and far more regression testing.**

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Sequential model | Early: static testing only; dynamic testing comes late |
| Iterative/incremental model | Static + dynamic testing at all levels in every iteration |
| Frequent increments | Fast feedback + extensive regression testing |
| Agile | Light documentation + high automation + experience-based manual testing |

## 1️⃣ These Rules Hold in **EVERY** SDLC

> Waterfall, V-model, spiral, Scrum, Kanban… **it makes no difference.** The four practices below are good testing practices independent of the model.

---

## 2️⃣ The Four Good Testing Practices

| # | Practice | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ✅ **For every software development activity there is a corresponding test activity** | So **all** development activities are subject to quality control |
| 2 | 🎯 **Different test levels have specific and different test objectives** | Testing is appropriately comprehensive while **redundancy** is avoided |
| 3 | ⏰ **Test analysis and design for a level begins during the corresponding development phase** | Adheres to the **principle of early testing** |
| 4 | 👀 **Testers review work products as soon as drafts are available** | Earlier testing and defect detection → supports **shift left** |

---

## 3️⃣ Concrete Example — ATM Cash Withdrawal

```
Requirements written   →  Tester reviews the requirement (practice 1 + 4)
       ↓
Design produced        →  System test analysis/design starts (practice 3)
       ↓
Code written           →  Component testing: is the balance calculation right?
       ↓
System assembled       →  System testing: end-to-end withdrawal
       ↓
Handover               →  Acceptance testing: can a bank customer actually use it?
```

Every level has a **different objective** → component testing looks at internal logic, acceptance testing looks at user needs. **Nothing is tested twice for the same reason.**

---

### ❌ These Are NOT Model-Independent Good Practices

* ❌ "Testing starts after coding is finished" → breaks the early testing principle
* ❌ "Every level reruns the same tests" → that is redundancy
* ❌ "Testers only read finished documents, never drafts" → the opposite of shift left
* ❌ "These rules only apply to Agile projects" → **no, they apply to all of them**

## 1️⃣ The Common Thread: Test-First

**TDD, ATDD and BDD** are similar **test-first** development approaches.

All three share:

* ✅ Tests are defined **before the code is written**
* ✅ They implement the **principle of early testing**
* ✅ They follow **shift left**
* ✅ They support an **iterative** development model
* ✅ The tests **persist as automated tests** → they protect code quality during future adaptation and refactoring

> 🔑 Testing is not an afterthought check → it is **the thing that directs development**.

---

## 2️⃣ How They Differ — The Exam's Dividing Line

| | **TDD** | **ATDD** | **BDD** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stands for** | Test-Driven Development | Acceptance Test-Driven Development | Behavior-Driven Development |
| **Tests derive from** | **Test cases** (instead of extensive software design) | **Acceptance criteria** | The desired **behavior** |
| **When?** | Immediately before coding | **As part of the system design process** | While the requirement is being discussed |
| **Language** | Code / unit tests | Acceptance criteria | **Natural language: Given / When / Then** |
| **Audience** | Developers | Developers + business analysts | **All stakeholders**, including non-technical ones |
| **Source** | Beck 2003 | Gärtner 2011 | Chelimsky 2010 |

---

## 3️⃣ The TDD Cycle

```
1. Write the test first   →  it fails (no code yet)
       ↓
2. Write code to satisfy it →  it passes ✅
       ↓
3. Refactor the tests and the code
       ↓
   Repeat
```

---

## 4️⃣ Concrete Example — Hotel Discount Rule

> Rule: discount applies only to bookings of **MORE than 3 nights**.

| Approach | How it is expressed |
|---|---|
| **TDD** | Unit test written first: `assert discount(4) == True` / `assert discount(3) == False` |
| **ATDD** | Acceptance criterion: "a 4-night booking gets the discount" → the test is derived from it |
| **BDD** | `Given a 3-night booking, When the price is calculated, Then no discount is applied` |

---

* ❌ **DDD** (Domain-Driven Design) → a design approach, not test-first
* ❌ **Kanban / Scrum** → work management frameworks
* ❌ **CI/CD** → delivery practices
* ❌ Unit tests written after the code

|---|---|---|

| **ATDD** | Acceptance criteria | Part of system design |

## 1️⃣ What Is DevOps?

**DevOps** = **development (including testing)** and **operations** working together toward a set of common goals.

* 🤝 It is an **organizational approach** — not just a toolset!
* 🧠 It requires a **cultural shift** → both functions are treated with **equal value**
* 🚀 It promotes **team autonomy**, **fast feedback**, **integrated toolchains**, **CI** (continuous integration) and **CD** (continuous delivery)
* 🏭 Result: build–test–release faster through a **DevOps delivery pipeline**

> 🔑 DevOps = **culture plus practice, not a tool**. Testing is an equal partner to operations.

---

## 2️⃣ ✅ Benefits from a Testing Perspective

| Benefit | What it means |
|---|---|
| ⚡ **Fast feedback** | Code quality, and whether a change adversely affects existing code, is visible at once |
| ⬅️ **CI promotes shift left** | Developers submit code **accompanied by component tests and static analysis** |
| 🖥️ **Stable test environments** | Automated processes like CI/CD make them easy to establish |
| 📊 **More visibility on non-functional characteristics** | Performance efficiency and reliability are measured continuously |
| 🤖 **Less repetitive manual testing** | Thanks to automation through the delivery pipeline |
| 🛡️ **Regression risk minimized** | Because of the **scale and range** of automated regression tests |

---

## 3️⃣ ❌ Risks and Challenges

* 🏗️ **The DevOps delivery pipeline must be defined and established**
* 🔧 **CI/CD tools must be introduced and maintained**
* 💸 **Test automation requires additional resources** → it can be hard to establish and maintain

---

## 4️⃣ ⚠️ The Sentence That Decides Questions

> Even with a high level of automated testing, **manual testing will still be needed** — especially **from the user's perspective**.

### ❌ These Statements About DevOps Are FALSE

* ❌ "DevOps removes the need for manual testing entirely"
* ❌ "DevOps is just a toolchain and has nothing to do with culture"
* ❌ "With DevOps you no longer need regression testing" → the opposite: **automated regression is its heart**
* ❌ "DevOps delays testing" → the opposite: **it promotes shift left**

---

## 5️⃣ Concrete Example — Smart Water Meter Reading System

```
Developer pushes code
    ↓
CI: automated build + static analysis + component tests   (shift left)
    ↓
Automated regression suite runs                            (regression risk ↓)
    ↓
Performance measurements reported                          (non-functional visibility ↑)
    ↓
CD: automatic deployment to a stable test environment
    ↓
Manual exploratory test: can a real user follow it?        (still needed!)
```

---

| **What it requires** | A cultural shift, equal value for both functions |
| **Technical practices** | CI, CD, integrated toolchains |

## 1️⃣ What Is Shift Left?

**Shift left** = performing testing **earlier** in the SDLC.

* ⏰ It is another name for the principle of early testing (see 1.3)
* 🚫 Do **not** wait for code to be implemented or components to be integrated
* ⚠️ **BUT**: it does **NOT** mean testing later in the SDLC should be neglected!

> 🔑 Shift left = **test early as well**, not "test only early".

---

## 2️⃣ The 5 Good Practices of Shift Left

| # | Practice | What it buys you |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 👀 **Reviewing the specification from a tester's perspective** | Finds potential defects: ambiguities, incompleteness, inconsistencies |
| 2 | ✍️ **Writing test cases before the code is written** and running the code in a **test harness** during implementation | Coding is driven by the tests |
| 3 | 🔁 **Using CI, and even better CD** | Fast feedback plus automated component tests when code hits the repository |
| 4 | 🔍 **Completing static analysis of source code before dynamic testing**, or as part of an automated process | Defects are found without executing the code |
| 5 | ⚡ **Performing non-functional testing starting at component test level where possible** | These types usually come **late** (they need a complete system and a representative environment) → pulling them forward is shift left |

---

## 3️⃣ The Price and the Payoff

```
Early in the process:  💸 Extra training + effort + cost
        ↓
Later in the process:  💰 Expected savings in effort and cost
```

* 🗣️ For this to work, **stakeholders must be convinced** and bought into the concept.

---

## 4️⃣ Example — Parcel Tracking System

| ✅ Shift left | ❌ NOT shift left |
|---|---|
| A tester reviews the "parcel status" requirement draft as soon as it exists | The tester waits until the whole system is assembled |
| The "delivered" test case is written before the code | Tests are written after the code is finished |
| Static analysis + component tests run automatically on every push | Static analysis is done once, just before release |
| API response time is measured at component level | Performance testing happens only during acceptance testing |
| | Assigning more testers to acceptance testing → **that is late, not a shift left** |

---

|---|---|

| **Which principle is it?** | Early testing (ISTQB principle 3) |
| **Does it cancel later testing?** | ❌ **No**, never |
| **Short-term effect?** | Extra training, effort, cost |
| **Long-term effect?** | Saved effort and cost |
| **Precondition?** | Stakeholders must be convinced |

* 📅 At the end of a **project or iteration**
* 🏁 At a **release milestone**
* 🆘 Or **whenever needed**

> ⚠️ Their timing and organization **depend on the SDLC model being followed.**

**Not** only testers!

* 👨‍💻 Developers
* 🏛️ Architects
* 📋 Product owner
* 📊 Business analysts

> 🔑 A retrospective is a **whole-team meeting**, not an internal test team huddle.

```

        ↓
2. What was not successful, and could be improved?
        ↓
3. How do we incorporate the improvements and retain the successes?
```

* 📝 Results **should be recorded** → normally part of the **test completion report** (see 5.3.2)

| | **Test level** | **Test type** |

* 🧩 The test object grows from a **single component** → a **complete system** → even a **system of systems**
* 🔗 Test levels are **related to other activities** within the SDLC
* 📏 **In sequential SDLC models:** the **exit criteria** of one level are part of the **entry criteria** of the next
* 🔁 **In some iterative models this may not apply**
* 🪢 A single development activity may **span multiple test levels**
* ⏱️ Test levels **may overlap in time**

## 1️⃣ The Five Test Levels — Master Table

| Level | Test object | Main objective | Test basis | Who performs it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Component (unit) testing** | A single component, **in isolation** | Is the internal logic correct? | Detailed design, code | **Developers**, in their own development environments |
| **2. Component integration testing** | **Interfaces and interactions between components** | Do the parts talk to each other? | Software design, architecture | Developers / testers |
| **3. System testing** | The **complete system or product** | End-to-end behavior and capabilities | System specifications | Often an **independent test team** |
| **4. System integration testing** | Interfaces between the system under test and **other systems and external services** | Can it talk to the outside world? | Interface specifications | Test team |
| **5. Acceptance testing** | The complete system, from the user's angle | **Validation** + readiness for deployment | Business needs, user requirements | **Ideally the intended users** |

---

## 2️⃣ The 5 Attributes That Distinguish Levels (memorize)

* 🧩 **Test object**
* 🎯 **Test objectives**
* 📋 **Test basis**
* 🐛 **Defects and failures**
* 👥 **Approach and responsibilities**

> 🔑 This list exists to **avoid overlapping of test activities**.

---

## 3️⃣ Which Defect Shows Up at Which Level?

| Defect type | Level |
|---|---|
| A fault in a module's **internal logic** | **Component testing** |
| **Communication / interface** faults between components | **Component integration testing** |
| **Business rules applied incorrectly** in the system | **System testing** |
| **User needs not met** | **Acceptance testing** |
| **Data mismatch with an external service** (bank POS, courier API) | **System integration testing** |

---

## 4️⃣ Level-Specific Details

* 🧪 **Component testing** needs specific support: **test harnesses**, **unit test frameworks**, **stubs and drivers**
* 🔗 **Component integration testing** depends heavily on the **integration strategy**: **bottom-up**, **top-down**, **big-bang**
* 🖥️ **System testing** covers both **functional** (end-to-end tasks) and **non-functional** testing. For some characteristics (e.g. **usability**) a **complete system in a representative test environment** is preferable. **Simulations** of sub-systems may be used.
* 🌐 **System integration testing** needs an environment **preferably similar to the operational one**
* 👤 Forms of **acceptance testing**: **user acceptance testing (UAT)**, **operational acceptance testing**, **contractual acceptance testing**, **regulatory acceptance testing**, **alpha testing**, **beta testing**

---

## 5️⃣ Concrete Example — University Course Registration System

```
The prerequisite-check unit is tested alone using stubs and drivers
    → COMPONENT TESTING
            ↓
Data exchange between the prerequisite unit and the capacity unit is tested
    → COMPONENT INTEGRATION TESTING
            ↓
A student logs in, picks courses and completes enrolment (end-to-end)
    → SYSTEM TESTING
            ↓
Does the system talk to the university payment system and the government portal?
    → SYSTEM INTEGRATION TESTING
            ↓
Real students and registry staff try it and sign it off
    → ACCEPTANCE TESTING
```

> 🔑 **Stubs/drivers + an isolated unit** → component testing. **The interface between two units** → component integration testing.

## 1️⃣ The Four Test Types — The Core Distinction

| Test type | Looks at | Question | Main objective |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Functional testing** | The **functions** the system should perform | **"WHAT does it do?"** | Functional **completeness**, **correctness**, **appropriateness** |
| **Non-functional testing** | Attributes **other than** functional ones | **"HOW WELL does it do it?"** | Checking the non-functional **quality characteristics** |
| **Black-box testing** | **Specification-based** — ignores internal structure | "Does it match the specification?" | Checking behavior **against the specification** |
| **White-box testing** | **Structure-based** — code, architecture, work flows, data flows | "How much of the structure is covered?" | **Covering the underlying structure to an acceptable level** |

> 🔑 **Functional ↔ non-functional** = *what* vs *how well*.
> 🔑 **Black-box ↔ white-box** = *specification-based* vs *structure-based*.
> ⚠️ These are **two independent axes!** One test can be both **functional** and **black-box** at the same time.

---

## 2️⃣ ISO/IEC 25010 — Non-functional Quality Characteristics

| # | Characteristic | Example test |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ⚡ **Performance efficiency** | Does the page load within 2 seconds? |
| 2 | 🔌 **Compatibility** | Does it work on Chrome, Safari and Android? |
| 3 | 🙋 **Usability** (also known as interaction capability) | Can a user find the add-to-cart button? |
| 4 | 🛡️ **Reliability** | Does it run 72 hours without interruption? |
| 5 | 🔒 **Security** | Can an unauthorized user see someone else's order? |
| 6 | 🔧 **Maintainability** | Can the code be changed easily? |
| 7 | 📦 **Portability** (also known as flexibility) | Can it be moved to a new cloud? |
| 8 | ☢️ **Safety** | Could a failure endanger human life? |

---

## 3️⃣ Critical Notes on Non-functional Testing

* ⏰ It is sometimes appropriate to **start early in the SDLC** (e.g. as part of reviews or component testing) → that is a form of **shift left**
* 🔁 **Many non-functional tests are derived from functional tests:** they use the same functional test but check whether a **non-functional constraint** holds while the function runs
* 🚨 **Late discovery of non-functional defects can pose a serious threat to the success of a project**
* 🧪 Sometimes a **very specific test environment** is required (e.g. a **usability lab** for usability testing)

---

## 4️⃣ Tell Them Apart — Smart Thermostat

| Test | Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Entering 22 °C sets the device to 22 °C | **Functional** | *What* it does |
| The display updates in **under 200 ms** after new temperature data arrives | **Non-functional** (performance efficiency) | *How well / how fast* it does it |
| A test case written from the requirements document | **Black-box** | Specification-based |
| Is every `if` branch in the temperature calculation covered? | **White-box** | Structure-based |

> ⚠️ **Trap:** if a timing constraint is measured *while* a function runs, the test is **non-functional, not functional.** Being derived from a functional test does not make it functional.

---

## 5️⃣ The Most Important Rule

> ✅ **All four test types can be applied at ALL test levels** — only the **focus** differs per level.
> ✅ **Different test techniques** can be used to derive test conditions and test cases for every one of these types.

---

| **Non-functional** | How well does it do it? | What / how well |
| **Black-box** | Driven by the specification, blind to internals | Source of information |
| **White-box** | Driven by code/structure, aiming at coverage | Source of information |

## 1️⃣ A Change First, Then Two Tests

A component or system typically changes for two reasons:

* ➕ **Enhancement** → adding a new feature
* 🔧 **Fix** → removing a defect

In both cases testing should include **confirmation testing** and **regression testing**.

---

## 2️⃣ The Core Comparison

| | **Confirmation testing** | **Regression testing** |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | "Is the original defect really fixed?" | "Did the change break **something else**?" |
| **Focus** | The **changed / fixed** area | The **unchanged** areas |
| **What is run** | Tests that previously **failed** because of the defect + **new tests** covering the fix | Previously **passing** tests that should not be affected |
| **Scope** | Narrow | Wide — the same component, other components in the same system, even **other connected systems** |
| **Environment relevant?** | No | ✅ Yes — it **may not be restricted to the test object; it can relate to the environment** |
| **Order** | **First** | **Second** |
| **Automation candidate?** | Less so | 🔴 **A strong candidate** |

> 🔑 **Confirmation** → "did the fix work?" **Regression** → "did the fix break anything?"

---

## 3️⃣ Confirmation Testing — How Much, Depending on Risk

| Risk / resources | How to test |
|---|---|
| Time and budget available, high risk | ✅ Execute **all** tests that failed due to the defect **and** add **new tests** covering the changes made to fix it |
| Time or money is short | ⚠️ Simply exercise the **test steps that reproduce the failure** and check that the failure **does not occur** |

---

## 4️⃣ Regression Testing — What You Must Know

* 🔍 It is advisable to perform an **impact analysis** first to recognize the extent of regression testing → **which parts of the software could be affected?**
* 🔁 Regression suites are run **many times** and the number of test cases **grows with each iteration or release** → a **strong candidate for automation**
* ⏰ Test automation **should start early in the project**
* 🏭 **Where CI is used (e.g. DevOps)** it is good practice to include automated regression tests in the pipeline → possibly **at different test levels**
* 📐 If defects are fixed and/or changes are made, confirmation and/or regression testing is needed **on all test levels**

---

## 5️⃣ Concrete Example — Podcast App

```
Defect: the download queue skips some episodes
        ↓
Developer fixes it
        ↓
STEP 1: Re-run the test case that exposed the failure
        → CONFIRMATION TESTING ✅
        ↓
STEP 2: Re-run the playlist and subscription module tests
        (these should not have been affected)
        → REGRESSION TESTING ✅
```

---

### ❌ Common Mistakes

* ❌ "Regression testing proves the defect is fixed" → no, that is **confirmation testing**
* ❌ "Confirmation testing sweeps the whole system" → no, that is **regression testing**
* ❌ "Regression only touches the changed component" → no, it can reach **other connected systems**
* ❌ "Regression first, then confirmation" → the order is **the other way round**

---

| Concept | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Confirmation testing** | Is the fixed defect really gone? |
| **Regression testing** | Did the change damage something that worked? |
| **Impact analysis** | Done first, to size the regression scope |
| **Automation** | Regression is the top candidate; start early |
| **Levels** | Both may be needed on **all test levels** |

## 1️⃣ What Is Maintenance Testing?

**Maintenance testing** = testing the changes made to a system that is already **operational**.

It covers two things at once:

* ✅ Evaluating the **success of the implementation** of the change → **confirmation testing**
* 🛡️ Checking for possible **regressions in the unchanged parts** of the system → **regression testing**

> 🔑 The unchanged part is **usually most of the system** → the bulk of maintenance testing is **regression**.

---

## 2️⃣ Categories of Maintenance (ISO/IEC 14764)

| Category | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 🔧 **Corrective** | Removing a defect | Wrong rounding of an exchange rate is fixed |
| 🔄 **Adaptive** | Adapting to changes in the environment | Supporting a new OS version |
| ⚡ **Performance / maintainability improvement** | Making it faster or easier to maintain | Query optimization, code refactoring |

So maintenance can involve:

* 📅 **Planned** releases / deployments
* 🚨 **Unplanned** releases / deployments → **hot fixes**

---

## 3️⃣ Impact Analysis

* 🧭 May be done **before** a change is made
* ❓ Purpose: decide **whether the change should be made at all**, based on the potential consequences in other areas of the system

---

## 4️⃣ What Determines the Scope of Maintenance Testing? (3 Items)

| # | Factor |
|---|---|
| 1 | ⚠️ The **degree of risk** of the change |
| 2 | 📏 The **size of the existing system** |
| 3 | 📐 The **size of the change** |

---

## 5️⃣ The Three Triggers — The Exam's Favourite

| Trigger | What it covers | Testing focus |
|---|---|---|
| 🔧 **Modifications** | Planned enhancements (release-based), corrective changes, **hot fixes** | Confirmation + regression |
| 🌐 **Upgrades or migrations of the operational environment** | Moving from one platform to another | Tests of the **new environment** + the **changed software** + **data conversion** tests |
| 🗄️ **Retirement** | An application reaching the end of its life | **Data archiving** tests (if long retention is required) + tests of **restore and retrieval** procedures |

---

## 6️⃣ Concrete Examples

| Situation | Trigger | What to test |
|---|---|---|
| A smart water meter system moves **from its own data centre to the cloud**; the code is unchanged, five years of readings are migrated | **Migration** | **Data conversion** first, then regression in the new environment |
| A currency conversion system must handle a **new rate format published by the central bank** | **Modification / adaptive maintenance** | Confirmation + regression |
| A vehicle fleet tracking system is **retired**, but historical data must be kept for the legal retention period | **Retirement** | **Data archiving** + **restore and retrieval** procedures |
| A **hot fix** ships overnight for a critical production crash | **Modification (unplanned)** | Confirmation + a fast regression pass |

---

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **When is maintenance testing done?** | On changes to a system that is **already operational** |
| **What does it include?** | Success of the change **+** regression in the unchanged parts |
| **The 3 scope drivers** | Degree of risk, size of the existing system, size of the change |
| **The 3 triggers** | Modifications · Upgrades/migrations · Retirement |
| **Special test for migration** | **Data conversion** |
| **Special test for retirement** | **Data archiving + restore and retrieval** |

## 1️⃣ What Is Static Testing?

**Static testing** means testing **without executing** the software. You read and examine the code, a process specification, the system architecture or any other work product.

| Method | How is it done? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Review** | Manual examination by people | The team reads the requirement specification |
| **Static analysis** | Automated examination by a tool | SonarQube scanning the code |

> 🔑 **Static testing** → reads without running, **Dynamic testing** → runs it and watches the behaviour

---

## 2️⃣ Objectives of Static Testing

- ⬆️ **Improving quality**
- 🐛 **Detecting defects**
- 📏 Assessing characteristics such as **readability, completeness, correctness, testability and consistency**

> ⚡ Static testing can be applied for both **verification** and **validation** — both, not one!

---

## 3️⃣ Static Testing Is Teamwork

Testers + business representatives (Product Owner, business analyst) + developers work together in:

- 🧩 **Example mapping**
- 📝 **Collaborative user story writing**
- 📋 **Backlog refinement sessions**

The goal: user stories meet the defined criteria, e.g. the **Definition of Ready**; they are complete, understandable and contain **testable acceptance criteria**.

By **asking the right questions**, testers explore, challenge and help improve the proposed user stories.

> 💡 Example — an "Add to cart" story in a web shop:
> The tester asks → "What happens when stock is zero?" → "What is the maximum quantity?"
> The story is fixed **before a line of code exists**. Nothing was executed!

---

## 4️⃣ Why Static Analysis Pays Off

- ⚡ Identifies problems **before dynamic testing**
- 💰 Requires **less effort** → no test cases needed, the tool does the work
- 🔁 Usually built into the **CI framework** → runs automatically on every commit
- 🔒 Finds more than code defects — it also evaluates **maintainability and security**
- ✍️ Spelling checkers and readability tools are static analysis tools too

---

| How is it done? | Reviews (people) + static analysis (tools) |
| What does it find? | **Defects directly** (not via failures) |
| Verification or validation? | **Both** |
| Are test cases needed? | **No** for static analysis |
| Where does it live? | Inside the **CI** pipeline |

## 1️⃣ The Golden Rule: If It Can Be Read and Understood, It Can Be Reviewed

> **Almost any work product** can be examined using static testing.

### ✅ These CAN be examined:
- 📋 **Requirement specification documents**
- 💻 **Source code**
- 📄 **Test plans**
- 🧪 **Test cases**
- 📦 **Product backlog items**
- 🗺️ **Test charters**
- 📁 **Project documentation**
- ✍️ **Contracts**
- 🏗️ **Models**

---

## 2️⃣ Two Methods, Two Different Conditions

| Method | What does it need? |
|---|---|
| **Review** | The work product must be **readable and understandable** — a human reads it |
| **Static analysis** | The work product needs a **structure it can be checked against** — a model, code, or text with a **formal syntax** |

> 🔑 If a person reads it → it must be **understandable**. If a tool scans it → it must have **structure**.

---

## 3️⃣ ❌ These CANNOT Be Examined by Static Testing

- 🔒 **3rd party executable code** → no source available, and for **legal reasons** it should not be analyzed
- 🤖 Work products that are **difficult for human beings to interpret** and **should not be analyzed by tools** (compiled binaries, encrypted content)

> ⚡ **Exam trap:** The question is always phrased "which work product is NOT suitable for static testing?"
> The answer is almost always **3rd party / compiled executable code**.
> Requirements, code, test cases, contracts, models, backlog items → **all of these can be reviewed**, so never pick them.

## 1️⃣ Why Static Testing Is Valuable

| Benefit | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ⏰ **Early detection** | Finds defects in the **earliest phases** of the SDLC → fulfils the **early testing principle** | A payroll requirement is fixed before coding starts |
| 🔍 **Sees what dynamic testing can't** | Some defects never surface by running the software | Unreachable code, design patterns not implemented as desired, defects in non-executable work products |
| 📊 **Evaluates quality** | Builds **confidence** in the work product | "This design document is solid, we can move on" |
| ✅ **Verifies requirements** | Stakeholders confirm the documented requirements describe their **actual needs** | The "this isn't what we asked for" risk disappears early |
| 🤝 **Shared understanding** | Creates one common picture among stakeholders | Analyst, developer and tester all understand the same thing |
| 🗣️ **Better communication** | Stakeholders talk early | This is why a **wide variety of stakeholders** should be involved |
| 💰 **Lower cost** | Reviews cost something, but the **overall project cost** is much lower | Fixing a defect later takes far more time and effort |
| ⚙️ **Fewer code defects** | Static analysis finds certain code defects **more efficiently** than dynamic testing | Lower overall development effort too |

> 🔑 **Find it early** → cause, **fix it cheaply** → effect

---

## 2️⃣ Defects Dynamic Testing Can NEVER Find

- 🚫 **Unreachable code** → it never runs, so it can never fail
- 🏗️ **Design patterns not implemented as desired**
- 📄 **Defects in non-executable work products** → requirements, contracts, test plans

---

## 3️⃣ ❌ These Are NOT Benefits of Static Testing

- ❌ **Triggering failures** → that is dynamic testing's job
- ❌ **Measuring performance efficiency** → the code has to run, so dynamic testing
- ❌ **Proving there are no defects left** → impossible (ISTQB Principle 1)
- ❌ **Finding the root cause and fixing the code** → that is debugging

| Which principle does it fulfil? | **Early testing** |
| What does it find? | **Defects directly**, not failures |
| Return on investment? | **Very high** — late fixes are expensive |
| Who should take part? | **As wide a variety of stakeholders as possible** |

## 1️⃣ They Are Not Rivals — They Complement Each Other

> Static and dynamic testing share the **same objective**: supporting the detection of defects in work products.
> But they find **different defects**. Neither replaces the other.

---

## 2️⃣ The Core Differences

| | **Static Testing** | **Dynamic Testing** |
|---|---|---|
| **Is the code run?** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| **What does it find?** | **Defects directly** | **Failures** first; the defect is determined by **subsequent analysis** |
| **Rarely executed paths** | ✅ Easy to reach | ❌ Hard to reach |
| **Non-executable work products** | ✅ Applicable (requirements, contracts) | ❌ Not applicable |
| **Quality characteristics measured** | Those **not dependent** on execution → **maintainability** | Those **dependent** on execution → **performance efficiency** |

> 🔑 **Static** → catches the **defect directly**, **Dynamic** → produces a **failure**, and you analyze your way back to the defect

---

## 3️⃣ Defects That Are Easier / Cheaper to Find Statically

| Defect type | Example |
|---|---|
| 📋 **Requirement defects** | Inconsistencies, ambiguities, contradictions, omissions, inaccuracies, duplications |
| 🏗️ **Design defects** | Inefficient database structures, poor modularization |
| 💻 **Certain coding defects** | Variables with undefined values, undeclared variables, **unreachable code**, duplicated code, excessive complexity |
| 📐 **Deviations from standards** | Not following naming conventions in the coding standard |
| 🔌 **Incorrect interface specifications** | Mismatched number, type or order of parameters |
| 🔒 **Security vulnerabilities** | Buffer overflows |
| 🎯 **Gaps in test basis coverage** | A missing test for an acceptance criterion |

---

## 4️⃣ Exam Drill — Which Test Finds It?

| Defect | Which test? | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| Two parts of the design specification contradict each other | **Static** | A document cannot be executed |
| Response time is so long that users lose patience | **Dynamic** | Performance requires execution |
| A path in the code is never reached during execution | **Static** | Unreachable code produces no failure |
| A variable is declared but never used | **Static** | A tool sees it by reading the code |
| The program generates the wrong report | **Dynamic** | Wrong behaviour only shows when it runs |

---

| Rule | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Static ≠ Dynamic** | Static reads, dynamic executes |
| **Static = defect directly** | No failure stage needed |
| **Dynamic = failure → analysis → defect** | Two steps |

| **Performance efficiency → dynamic** | Dependent on execution |

## 1️⃣ The Core Idea

> Stakeholder feedback must come **early** and **often**.
> Late feedback is expensive feedback.

---

## 2️⃣ ✅ Benefits of Early and Frequent Feedback

- ⚡ **Potential quality problems are communicated early**
- 🧠 **Misunderstandings about requirements are prevented**
- 🔄 **Changes to requirements are understood and implemented earlier**
- 👨‍💻 **The development team understands better what they are building**
- 🎯 The team focuses on the features that **deliver the most value** and have the **most positive impact on identified risks**

---

## 3️⃣ ❌ What Happens With Little Stakeholder Involvement?

The product does not meet the stakeholder's **original or current vision**. The result:

| Consequence | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 💸 **Costly rework** | Finished work is thrown away and rewritten |
| 📅 **Missed deadlines** | Rework eats the schedule |
| 😤 **Blame games** | "You asked for this" / "No, you misunderstood us" |
| 💀 **Complete project failure** | The worst case |

---

## 4️⃣ A Concrete Example — Hotel Booking System

```
The stakeholder saw nothing for 6 months
    ↓
The team coded "discount for 3 nights and above"
    ↓
Demo day, the stakeholder says: "No, it was MORE THAN 3 nights!"
    ↓
Six months of pricing engine gets rewritten 💸
```

With early feedback, a **one-sentence** correction in the first sprint demo would have been enough.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Feedback | Outcome |
|---|---|
| **Early + frequent** | No misunderstandings, cheap changes, focus on the right features |
| **Late + rare** | Rework, delays, blame, project failure |

> 🔑 **Early feedback** → cause, **the right product and cheap changes** → effect

## 1️⃣ Where Does the Review Process Come From?

- 📘 Standard: **ISO/IEC 20246**
- 🧩 A structured but **flexible framework** that can be tailored to the situation
- ⚖️ The **more formal** the review, the **more of the tasks** in each activity are performed
- 🔁 Most work products are too large for a single review → the process may be **invoked multiple times**

---

## 2️⃣ The 5 Activities — In Order

| # | Activity | Question | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Planning** | *What, why, against which criteria?* | The scope is defined: purpose, work product to be reviewed, **quality characteristics** to evaluate, areas to focus on, **exit criteria**, standards, effort and timeframes |
| 2 | **Review initiation** | *Is everyone ready?* | Every participant **has access to the work product**, **understands their role and responsibilities** and receives everything needed |
| 3 | **Individual review** | *Let everyone examine it alone* | Each reviewer reviews **on their own**, applying review techniques (checklist-based, scenario-based) and **logs anomalies, recommendations and questions** |
| 4 | **Communication and analysis** | *Are these anomalies really defects?* | Anomalies are **discussed and analyzed**; for each one a decision is made on **status, ownership and required actions**. Usually in a **review meeting**, where the quality level and follow-up actions are also decided. A **follow-up review** may be needed |
| 5 | **Fixing and reporting** | *Fix it, close it, report it* | A **defect report** is created for every defect; once the **exit criteria** are met the work product is **accepted**; the results are **reported** |

---

## 3️⃣ ⚡ The Exam's Favourite Trap

> **Anomaly ≠ Defect!**
> What reviewers log during the individual review are **anomalies**. Whether they are defects is decided in **Communication and analysis**.

> 🔑 If the question says "the reviewers have finished examining the document individually — **what comes next?**" → the answer is **Communication and analysis**

---

## 🧠 Summary Flow

```
Planning (scope, exit criteria)
    ↓
Review initiation (everyone ready, access granted)
    ↓
Individual review (anomalies logged)
    ↓
Communication and analysis (anomaly → defect? meeting, decisions)
    ↓
Fixing and reporting (defect reports, exit criteria, acceptance)
```

## 1️⃣ The Roles Table — This Is the One to Memorize

| Role | The job in one sentence | Keyword |
|---|---|---|
| 👔 **Manager** | Decides **what** is to be reviewed and provides **resources** (staff, time) | Decision + **resources** |
| ✍️ **Author** | **Creates and fixes** the work product under review | **Produces + fixes** |
| 🕊️ **Moderator / Facilitator** | Ensures the **effective running of review meetings**: mediation, time management, a **safe environment where everyone can speak freely** | **Runs the meeting** |
| 🖊️ **Scribe / Recorder** | **Collates anomalies** from reviewers and **records decisions and new anomalies** found during the meeting | **Writes it down** |
| 🔍 **Reviewer** | **Performs the review**. May be someone working on the project, a subject matter expert, or any other stakeholder | **Examines** |
| 🧭 **Review leader** | Takes **overall responsibility** for the review: **who is involved**, **when and where** it takes place | **Organizes** |

> ℹ️ More detailed roles are described in the ISO/IEC 20246 standard.

---

## 2️⃣ ⚠️ The Pair People Mix Up Most

| | **Moderator (Facilitator)** | **Review Leader** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | **The meeting itself** | **The whole review** |
| **Does** | Mediation, time management, safe environment | Decides who is involved, arranges when and where |
| **When?** | **During** the meeting | **Before** it, as organization |

> 🔑 **Moderator** → **runs** the meeting, **Review leader** → **sets up** the review

Another frequent mix-up: the **scribe records** anomalies ✍️, the **reviewer finds** them 🔍.

---

| Task description | Role |
|---|---|
| "Ensures effective meetings and a safe review environment" | **Moderator / Facilitator** |
| "Records decisions and new anomalies found in the meeting" | **Scribe** |
| "Decides who will be involved and when the review takes place" | **Review leader** |
| "Decides what is reviewed and allocates staff and time" | **Manager** |
| "Wrote the product and will fix the defects found" | **Author** |
| "Examines the document and identifies anomalies" | **Reviewer** |

| Success factor | Why it matters |

| 🎯 **Clear objectives and measurable exit criteria** | You know when the review is done |
