## 1️⃣ What Is a Test Technique For?

Test techniques help the tester answer **two questions**:

| Activity | Question | What the technique gives you |
|---|---|---|
| **Test analysis** | **What** to test? | Test conditions, coverage items |
| **Test design** | **How** to test? | Test cases, test data |

> 🔑 The goal: produce a **small but sufficient** set of test cases **systematically**. Not random testing, methodical testing.

---

## 2️⃣ Three Families: Black-box / White-box / Experience-based

| | **Black-box** | **White-box** | **Experience-based** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Also called** | Specification-based | Structure-based | — |
| **Looks at** | External **behavior** | Internal **code/structure** | The tester's **knowledge and intuition** |
| **Based on** | Requirements, user stories | Source code, control flow graph | Past defects, domain knowledge |
| **When written?** | Can be **before** the code exists | Only **after** design or implementation | Any time |
| **If the code changes?** | Behavior unchanged → tests **still useful** ✅ | Tests must be **rewritten** ❌ | Changes |
| **Examples** | Equivalence partitioning, BVA, decision tables, state transition | Statement testing, branch testing | Error guessing, exploratory testing, checklists |

> 🔑 **Black-box** → "what does it do?", **White-box** → "how does it do it?", **Experience** → "where will it break?"

---

## 3️⃣ The Distinctions the Exam Asks About

### ✅ Black-box ≠ White-box
- Black-box testing **never looks inside** → tests survive an implementation change
- White-box testing **depends on the code** → you cannot write it without the code

### ✅ Decision table testing ≠ Branch testing
- **Decision table** = black-box, combinations of conditions from the **requirements**
- **Branch testing** = white-box, decision outcomes in the **code**
- Both involve "conditions", but one comes from a document and one from reading code

### ✅ What makes experience-based techniques special
- Their effectiveness depends **entirely on the tester's skill**
- They can find defects that black-box and white-box techniques **miss**
- So they **complement** the other techniques rather than replace them

---

## 4️⃣ Which Technique, When?

| Situation | Technique that fits |
|---|---|
| Requirement says "if total exceeds $100, give 5% discount" | **Equivalence partitioning + boundary value analysis** |
| The requirement combines several conditions | **Decision table testing** |
| The object changes state on events (booking, session) | **State transition testing** |
| I need to measure how much of the code I tested | **Statement / branch coverage** |
| No specification, no time, but I know the domain | **Exploratory testing** |

---

| Family | Based on | Coverage measurable? | Code needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Black-box** | Specification | ✅ Yes (partitions, boundaries, columns, transitions) | ❌ No |
| **White-box** | Code structure | ✅ Yes (statements, branches) | ✅ Yes |
| **Experience-based** | Human experience | ⚠️ Hard / not formal | ❌ No |

## 📦 What Is in This Section?

Black-box techniques look only at **what the test object should do**, never at **how it is built**. Four techniques are covered:

- 🧩 **Equivalence Partitioning** → Group values that behave the same, test one value per group
- 📏 **Boundary Value Analysis** → Test the edges of those groups, that is where defects hide
- 📋 **Decision Table Testing** → Test combinations of conditions, column by column
- 🔄 **State Transition Testing** → Test states and the transitions between them

> 🔑 What all four share: test cases are derived from the **specification**, never from the code.
4.2.1:
## 1️⃣ The Idea Is Simple

Split the input values into **groups you expect to be treated the same way**. These groups are **equivalence partitions**.

> 💡 The theory: if **one value** from a partition finds a defect, **every other value in that partition** would find the same defect.
> Therefore **one test per partition is enough**.

---

## 2️⃣ Rules for Partitions

| Rule | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ❌ **No overlap** | A value belongs to exactly one partition |
| ❌ **Never empty** | Every partition must contain at least one value |
| ✅ **Applies to any data** | Inputs, outputs, configuration items, internal values, time-related values, interface parameters |
| ✅ **Any kind** | Continuous/discrete, ordered/unordered, finite/infinite |

### 🟢 Valid partition
Values the system **should process**.

### 🔴 Invalid partition
Values the system **should reject or ignore**.

> ⚠️ Exam trap: **invalid partitions count towards coverage too!** 100% coverage means you tested them as well.

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example — Smart Thermostat 🌡️

The user enters a target temperature as an integer:

| Partition | Range | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | target < 5 | ❌ Input rejected (invalid) |
| **P2** | 5 – 15 | Frost protection |
| **P3** | 16 – 23 | Comfort |
| **P4** | 24 – 30 | Fast heating |
| **P5** | target > 30 | ❌ Input rejected (invalid) |

**Total partitions = 5** → 5 coverage items

### The tester ran these values: `3, 12, 20, 27, 29`

| Value | Which partition? |
|---|---|
| 3 | P1 ✅ |
| 12 | P2 ✅ |
| 20 | P3 ✅ |
| 27 | P4 ✅ |
| 29 | P4 ⚠️ (already covered — **wasted test**) |

**Partitions exercised = 4** (P1, P2, P3, P4). **P5 was never tested.**

### 🧮 Coverage Formula

```
Coverage = (partitions exercised / total partitions) × 100

         = (4 / 5) × 100 = 80%
```

> 🔑 Five tests were run, yet coverage is not 100%. **Two tests landed in the same partition** and one partition was never touched.
> **Number of tests ≠ coverage.** What counts is how many **distinct partitions** you hit.

---

## 4️⃣ Several Sets of Partitions → Each Choice Coverage

When a form has **two variables**, each variable has **its own set of partitions**.

> 💡 Example — property search form:
> - **Floor**: ground / first / second+ → 3 partitions
> - **Garden**: none / small / large → 3 partitions

**Each Choice coverage** = exercise every partition from every set **at least once**.

```
TC1: ground floor + large garden
TC2: first floor  + no garden
TC3: second+ floor + small garden
↓
3 test cases → all 3 partitions in both sets covered ✅
```

> 🔑 Each Choice **ignores combinations**. Instead of 3×3 = 9 combinations, **3 tests** are enough.
> Tests needed = **size of the largest set of partitions**.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What is the coverage item?** | The equivalence partition itself |
| **What does 100% coverage mean?** | Every partition, invalid ones included, exercised at least once |
| **Formula** | partitions exercised / total partitions × 100 |
| **Tests per partition?** | 1 is enough |
| **Simplest criterion with several sets** | Each Choice coverage |
| **Does Each Choice need combinations?** | ❌ No |

## 1️⃣ What Is BVA and Why Does It Work?

**Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)** exercises the **edges** of equivalence partitions.

* 📏 A partition's **minimum** and **maximum** values are its **boundary values**
* ⚠️ BVA works **only on ordered partitions** — "red / blue / green" has no edges
* 🐛 Why the edges? That is where developers slip: `>` instead of `>=`, a boundary shifted by one, a boundary left out entirely

> 🔑 BVA sits **on top of equivalence partitioning**. Find the partitions first, **then** test their edges.

---

## 2️⃣ 🚨 THE CRITICAL PART: How Many Boundaries? How Do You Count?

Two things get mixed up:

| Term | Meaning | Example (0–49 / 50–74) |
|---|---|---|
| **Boundary** | The **line where two partitions meet** | The line between 49 and 50 → **1 boundary** |
| **Boundary value** | A partition's **min or max** — an actual number | 49 and 50 → **2 boundary values** |

> 🔑 **ISTQB counts coverage items as boundary VALUES, not boundaries.**

### 📐 The Counting Rule (memorize it)

```
Each partition   → 1 min + 1 max = 2 boundary values
n ordered partitions → 2 × n boundary values
EXCEPTION: an open-ended (infinite) partition → NO boundary value on that side → only 1
```

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example — Exam Grading System 🎓

Score is an **integer from 0 to 100**:

| Partition | Score range | Grade |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | 0 – 49 | Fail |
| **P2** | 50 – 74 | Pass |
| **P3** | 75 – 100 | Distinction |

### 🧮 Count the boundary values:

| Partition | min | max |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **0** | **49** |
| P2 | **50** | **74** |
| P3 | **75** | **100** |

```
3 partitions × 2 = 6 boundary values → {0, 49, 50, 74, 75, 100}
```

Note: there are **2 boundaries** (P1|P2 and P2|P3) but **6 boundary values**. That is exactly what the exam asks.

---

## 4️⃣ 2-Value BVA

> **Two coverage items per boundary value:** the boundary value itself **+ its closest neighbor in the adjacent partition**

| Boundary value | Coverage items |
|---|---|
| 49 (max of P1) | 49, **50** |
| 50 (min of P2) | 50, **49** |
| 74 (max of P2) | 74, **75** |
| 75 (min of P3) | 75, **74** |

⚠️ **Watch out:** 49's neighbor is 50 and 50's neighbor is 49 — you write **the same pair twice**. So:

> 🔑 **In 2-value BVA the number of distinct test values = the number of boundary values.** Here **6**: `0, 49, 50, 74, 75, 100`

### 🧮 Coverage Formula

```
Coverage = (boundary values exercised / total boundary values) × 100
```

**Example:** the tester ran only `0, 50, 74, 100`:

```
Coverage = (4 / 6) × 100 = 66.7%
Missing  : 49 and 75
```

---

## 5️⃣ 3-Value BVA

> **Three coverage items per boundary value:** the boundary value **+ both of its neighbors** (one below, one above)

| Boundary value | Coverage items |
|---|---|
| 0 | **-1**, 0, **1** |
| 49 | **48**, 49, **50** |
| 50 | **49**, 50, **51** |
| 74 | **73**, 74, **75** |
| 75 | **74**, 75, **76** |
| 100 | **99**, 100, **101** |

```
6 boundary values × 3 = 18 coverage items (duplicates included)
Distinct test values: -1, 0, 1, 48, 49, 50, 51, 73, 74, 75, 76, 99, 100, 101  → 14 values
```

> ⚠️ In 3-value BVA some coverage items are **not boundary values** at all (48, 51, 73, 76). That is expected — ISTQB states it explicitly.

---

## 6️⃣ 2-Value ≠ 3-Value — Why the Difference Matters

| | **2-value BVA** | **3-value BVA** |
|---|---|---|
| **Coverage items per boundary** | **2** (boundary + adjacent neighbor) | **3** (boundary + both neighbors) |
| **Test values in our example** | 6 | 14 |
| **Rigor** | Lower | **Higher** |
| **Cost** | Cheap | Expensive |

### 🐛 The classic ISTQB example — what 3-value catches

```
Required code  : if (x <= 10) ...
Implemented    : if (x == 10) ...        ← DEFECT

2-value BVA → x = 10, x = 11
   x = 10  → TRUE in both versions   ✅ no difference, defect hidden
   x = 11  → FALSE in both versions  ✅ no difference, defect hidden
   → DEFECT NOT FOUND ❌

3-value BVA → adds x = 9
   x = 9   → TRUE in correct code, FALSE in the defective code
   → DEFECT FOUND ✅
```

> 🔑 **3-value BVA can detect defects that 2-value BVA overlooks.** Not the other way around.

---

## 7️⃣ Counting With Open-Ended Partitions — Password Example 🔐

A password is valid when its length is 6–12 characters. Length cannot be negative, and there is no stated upper limit.

| Partition | Range | min | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 Too short | 0 – 5 | **0** | **5** |
| P2 Correct | 6 – 12 | **6** | **12** |
| P3 Too long | 13 – ∞ | **13** | ❌ none (infinite) |

```
Boundary values = 0, 5, 6, 12, 13  → 5 of them (not 6!)
```

> 🔑 **A partition that runs to infinity contributes no boundary value on that side.** 2×3=6 becomes **5**. This is the exam's favorite trap.

---

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Which partitions can BVA use?** | Only **ordered** ones |
| **What is a boundary value?** | A partition's min or max |
| **n ordered partitions → how many boundary values?** | **2n** (minus open-ended sides) |
| **2-value BVA — coverage items per boundary** | **2**: boundary + closest neighbor in the adjacent partition |
| **3-value BVA — coverage items per boundary** | **3**: boundary + both neighbors |
| **Coverage formula** | coverage items exercised / total coverage items × 100 |
| **Which is more rigorous?** | **3-value** |
| **What does 3-value catch?** | Defects like `x==10` instead of `x<=10` (via x=9) |

## 1️⃣ What Is a Decision Table For?

When the requirement says **"if this condition AND this condition AND this condition, then do that"** → use a decision table.

* 📋 **Rows** → conditions (top) and actions (bottom)
* 📊 **Columns** → each column is a **decision rule**: a unique combination of conditions plus its outcome
* 🎯 The most effective way to record complex **business rules**

---

## 2️⃣ The Notation (the exam asks about this)

| Symbol | Where? | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | Condition row | The condition **is satisfied** |
| **F** | Condition row | The condition **is not satisfied** |
| **–** | Condition row | The condition's value is **irrelevant** to the outcome |
| **N/A** | Condition row | The condition is **infeasible** for that rule |
| **X** | Action row | The action **should occur** |
| *(blank)* | Action row | The action **should not occur** |

### Two kinds of table

| Kind | Values |
|---|---|
| **Limited-entry** | All conditions and actions are **Boolean** (T/F) |
| **Extended-entry** | Conditions may take **multiple values** (number ranges, equivalence partitions, discrete values) |

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example — Gym Membership Discount 🏋️

Three Boolean conditions → **full table = 2³ = 8 columns**

| | **R1** | **R2** | **R3** | **R4** | **R5** | **R6** | **R7** | **R8** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C1: Annual membership** | T | T | T | T | F | F | F | F |
| **C2: Student ID** | T | T | F | F | T | T | F | F |
| **C3: Paid up front** | T | F | T | F | T | F | T | F |
| **Action: Discount** | 35% | 25% | 20% | 10% | 15% | 10% | 5% | 0% |

> 💡 The pattern: condition 1 flips every 4 columns, condition 2 every 2, condition 3 every 1. That way no combination is skipped.

### 🧮 Coverage Item and Formula

> **Coverage item = the COLUMNS containing feasible combinations of conditions**

```
Coverage = (columns exercised / total feasible columns) × 100
```

**Tests that were run:**

| Test | C1 | C2 | C3 | Which rule? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TC1 | T | T | T | R1 ✅ |
| TC2 | T | F | F | R4 ✅ |
| TC3 | F | T | T | R5 ✅ |
| TC4 | F | F | F | R8 ✅ |
| TC5 | T | T | T | R1 ⚠️ repeat |

```
Distinct columns exercised = 4 (R1, R4, R5, R8)
Total columns              = 8
Coverage = (4 / 8) × 100 = 50%

Missing columns: R2, R3, R6, R7
```

> 🔑 Five tests, yet 50% coverage — **one test repeated a column**. Coverage counts **columns, not tests**.

---

## 4️⃣ Shrinking the Table

| Method | What it does | Effect on the denominator |
|---|---|---|
| **Delete infeasible columns** | Combinations that cannot occur are removed | **Denominator shrinks** |
| **Merge columns** | Conditions that do not affect the outcome become `–` and columns merge | Denominator shrinks |

> 💡 Example: "has a student ID" and "is a pensioner over 65" cannot both be true → that column is deleted.
> One of 8 columns removed → the denominator is now **7**, not 8. 100% coverage = all 7 columns.

> ⚠️ Decision table **minimization algorithms** are OUT OF SCOPE for CTFL.

---

## 5️⃣ Strengths and Weaknesses

### ✅ Strengths
- A systematic approach that **misses no combination**
- Exposes **gaps and contradictions** in the requirements
- Makes complex business logic readable

### ❌ Weakness
- The number of rules grows **exponentially** with conditions: 3 conditions → 8, 5 → 32, 10 → **1024** columns
- Remedy: a **minimized decision table** or a **risk-based approach**

---

## 6️⃣ Exam Distinction: Decision Table ≠ Branch Testing

| | **Decision table testing** | **Branch testing** |
|---|---|---|
| **Family** | Black-box | White-box |
| **Source** | Requirement / business rule | Source code / control flow graph |
| **Coverage item** | **Columns** of the table | **Branches** in the code |

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What are the rows?** | Conditions + actions |
| **What are the columns?** | Decision rules |
| **Coverage item?** | Columns with feasible combinations of conditions |
| **Formula** | columns exercised / feasible columns × 100 |
| **n Boolean conditions → how many columns?** | 2ⁿ in a full table |
| **What does `–` mean?** | The condition does not affect the outcome |
| **What does `N/A` mean?** | The condition is infeasible for that rule |

## 1️⃣ State Diagram and State Table

Some systems have **memory**: the same event produces a different result depending on **which state** the system is in. We model and test those with state models.

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **State** | The system's current condition (e.g. "Confirmed") |
| **Event** | What triggers a transition (e.g. "Pay") |
| **Guard condition** | What must hold for the transition to happen (e.g. `[N < 2]`) |
| **Action** | What the software does during the transition (e.g. `N := N + 1`) |
| **Transition** | A jump from one state to another — assumed **instantaneous** |

**Labeling syntax:** `event [guard condition] / action`

### 📊 State table ≠ State diagram (but equivalent)

| | **State diagram** | **State table** |
|---|---|---|
| **Layout** | — | Rows = states, Columns = events |
| **Invalid transitions** | ❌ Not shown | ✅ Shown as **empty cells** |

> 🔑 To count invalid transitions, read the **state table**, not the diagram.

---

## 2️⃣ Worked Example — Hotel Room Booking 🏨

**4 states, 5 events.** State table:

| State \ Event | Available | NotAvailable | ChangeRoom | Cancel | Pay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S1 Requested** | S2 | S3 | | | |
| **S2 Confirmed** | | | S1 | S4 | S4 |
| **S3 Waitlisted** | S2 | | | S4 | |
| **S4 End** | | | | | |

### 🧮 Count

```
Total cells       = 4 states × 5 events = 20
Filled cells      = 2 + 3 + 2 + 0       = 7   → VALID transitions
Empty cells       = 20 - 7              = 13  → INVALID transitions
Number of states  = 4
```

---

## 3️⃣ Three Coverage Criteria — With Formulas

### 🟢 All States Coverage
> **Coverage item = the states**

```
Coverage = (states exercised / total states) × 100
```

### 🟡 Valid Transitions Coverage (**0-switch coverage**)
> **Coverage item = single valid transitions**

```
Coverage = (valid transitions exercised / total valid transitions) × 100
```
**The most widely used criterion.**

### 🔴 All Transitions Coverage
> **Coverage item = EVERY cell in the state table** (valid + invalid)

```
Coverage = (transitions exercised or attempted / total valid+invalid transitions) × 100
```
Valid transitions are **exercised**, invalid ones are **attempted** (the system must reject them).

> ⚠️ Test **only ONE invalid transition per test case** → this avoids **defect masking**, where one defect hides another.

---

## 4️⃣ Let's Do the Arithmetic

**TC1:** `S1 --Available--> S2 --Pay--> S4`

| Criterion | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| All states | S1, S2, S4 exercised → 3/4 | **75%** |
| Valid transitions | 2 exercised → 2/7 | **28.6%** |
| All transitions | 2 exercised → 2/20 | **10%** |

**Add TC2:** `S1 --NotAvailable--> S3 --Available--> S2 --Cancel--> S4`

| Criterion | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| All states | S1,S2,S3,S4 → 4/4 | **100%** ✅ |
| Valid transitions | S1→S2, S2→S4(Pay), S1→S3, S3→S2, S2→S4(Cancel) = 5/7 | **71.4%** |
| All transitions | 5/20 | **25%** |

> 🔑 **You hit 100% all states coverage while valid transitions coverage is still 71%.** That is exactly why all states coverage is **weaker**.

---

## 5️⃣ The Strength Hierarchy (memorize it)

```
All Transitions Coverage
       ⊃  (guarantees)
Valid Transitions Coverage (0-switch)
       ⊃  (guarantees)
All States Coverage
```

| Statement | True? |
|---|---|
| 100% valid transitions → 100% all states | ✅ Yes, guaranteed |
| 100% all states → 100% valid transitions | ❌ No |
| 100% all transitions → 100% of both others | ✅ Yes |
| All transitions coverage is the **minimum** for safety-critical software | ✅ Yes |

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Criterion | Coverage item | Total in our example | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All states** | States | 4 | **Weakest** |
| **Valid transitions (0-switch)** | Valid transitions | 7 | **Most used** |
| **All transitions** | Valid + invalid | 20 | **Strongest**, minimum for critical software |

## 🔍 What Is in This Section?

White-box techniques look at the **internal structure of the code**. Because they are popular and simple, the syllabus covers **two code-related techniques**:

- 💻 **Statement testing** → How many lines of code were executed?
- 🔀 **Branch testing** → How many decision outcomes were exercised?

### ❌ Out of scope for this syllabus
- More **rigorous** code coverage techniques used in safety-critical environments (e.g. MC/DC)
- White-box techniques at higher test levels (e.g. **API testing**)
- Coverage not related to code (e.g. **neuron coverage** in neural network testing)

> 🔑 At CTFL level the exam only makes you calculate **statement** and **branch** coverage.
4.3.1:
## 1️⃣ Coverage Item: The Executable Statement

> **In statement testing the coverage items are executable statements**

```
Statement Coverage = (statements exercised / total executable statements) × 100
```

⚠️ Comments, blank lines and pure declarations **do not count**.

---

## 2️⃣ Worked Example — Discount Calculation 💰

```
1   function calculate_discount(amount, member):
2       discount = 0
3       if amount > 100:
4           discount = 5
5       if member:
6           discount = discount + 10
7       return discount
```

### 🧮 Count the executable statements

| Line | Statement | Counts? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Function header | ❌ |
| 2 | `discount = 0` | ✅ |
| 3 | `if amount > 100` | ✅ |
| 4 | `discount = 5` | ✅ |
| 5 | `if member` | ✅ |
| 6 | `discount = discount + 10` | ✅ |
| 7 | `return discount` | ✅ |

**Total executable statements = 6**

### Test 1: `amount = 150, member = Yes`

```
Lines executed: 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7   (6 statements)

Coverage = (6 / 6) × 100 = 100% ✅
```

### Test 2: `amount = 50, member = No`

```
Lines executed: 2 → 3 → 5 → 7           (4 statements)
Not executed  : 4, 6

Coverage = (4 / 6) × 100 = 66.7%
```

---

## 3️⃣ What 100% Statement Coverage DOES and DOES NOT Mean

### ✅ It guarantees
- **Every executable statement ran at least once**
- Every statement containing a defect **was executed** → a failure **may** have been triggered

### ❌ It does NOT guarantee
- ❌ That **all decision logic was tested** → some branches may be untaken
- ❌ That **data-dependent defects were found** → e.g. a division by zero only fails when the denominator is 0; the statement ran but nothing broke
- ❌ That **no defects remain**
- ❌ **100% branch coverage** → Test 1 above gives 100% statement coverage but only 50% branch coverage (see 4.3.2)

> 🔑 **Executing a statement ≠ seeing its defect.** A line running does not expose the defect in that line.

---

## 4️⃣ Exam Trap: Coverage Percentages Do NOT Add Up

> 💡 If test T1 gives 40% and test T2 gives 65% statement coverage:

| Statement | True? |
|---|---|
| Together they give 105% | ❌ Impossible |
| Together they give **at least 65%** | ✅ Certainly true |
| Together they give at most 100% | ✅ True |
| T2 covers every statement T1 covers | ❌ Unknowable — they may hit different lines |

> 💡 Same logic: **three tests** each giving **50%** coverage can together give **100%**. The tests **re-cover the same statements** — coverage **overlaps**, it does not sum.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Coverage item** | Executable statements |
| **Formula** | statements exercised / total executable statements × 100 |
| **What does 100% guarantee?** | Every statement ran at least once |
| **What does it NOT guarantee?** | Branch coverage, decision logic, data-dependent defects, absence of defects |
| **Do percentages add up?** | ❌ No, they overlap |

## 1️⃣ What Is a Branch?

> **A branch is a transfer of control between two nodes in the control flow graph.**

The control flow graph shows the possible sequences in which statements execute. Every **arrow (edge)** in that graph is a branch.

| Kind of branch | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Unconditional** | Straight-line code, no decision | Flow from line 1 to line 2 |
| **Conditional** | A decision outcome | `if` → TRUE branch / FALSE branch |

### Where conditional branches typically come from
- 🔀 The **true** or **false** outcome of an `if...then` decision
- 🔢 Each outcome of a `switch/case` statement
- 🔁 The decision to **exit** or **continue** a loop

---

## 2️⃣ Coverage Item and Formula

> **In branch testing the coverage items are branches**

```
Branch Coverage (BCov) = (X / Y) × 100%

X = number of branches exercised by the test cases
Y = total number of branches
```

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example 1 — Counting From a Control Flow Graph 📐

Seven nodes (N1–N7) and these directed edges:

```
N1 → N2
N2 → N3
N3 → N2      (loop back)
N2 → N4
N4 → N5
N4 → N6
N5 → N7
N6 → N7
```

### 🧮 The counting rule: **branches = edges**

```
Count the edges: 8 arrows

→ Coverage items = 8
→ 100% branch coverage requires all 8 branches to be exercised
```

> 🔑 **Do not count nodes, count ARROWS.** There are 7 nodes but the answer is **8**.

---

## 4️⃣ Worked Example 2 — Statement vs Branch on the Same Code 💰

```
1   function calculate_discount(amount, member):
2       discount = 0
3       if amount > 100:
4           discount = 5
5       if member:
6           discount = discount + 10
7       return discount
```

### Count the branches

| Decision | TRUE branch | FALSE branch |
|---|---|---|
| Line 3: `amount > 100` | 3 → 4 ✅ | 3 → 5 ✅ |
| Line 5: `member` | 5 → 6 ✅ | 5 → 7 ✅ |

**Total branches = 4**

### Test 1: `amount = 150, member = Yes`

```
Branches exercised : 3→4 (TRUE), 5→6 (TRUE)  = 2 branches
Not exercised      : 3→5 (FALSE), 5→7 (FALSE)

Statement coverage = 6/6 = 100%  ✅
Branch coverage    = 2/4 = 50%   ⚠️
```

### Add Test 2: `amount = 50, member = No`

```
Branches exercised : 3→5 (FALSE), 5→7 (FALSE)

Total branch coverage = 4/4 = 100% ✅
```

> 🔑 **One test reached 100% statement coverage but only 50% branch coverage.** This is the exam's favorite situation.

---

## 5️⃣ 🚨 Branch Coverage SUBSUMES Statement Coverage

```
100% Branch Coverage  ──guarantees──>  100% Statement Coverage  ✅
100% Statement Coverage ──guarantees──>  100% Branch Coverage   ❌
```

| Statement | True? |
|---|---|
| Any test set achieving 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage | ✅ |
| Any test set achieving 100% statement coverage also achieves 100% branch coverage | ❌ |
| Branch coverage is stronger than statement coverage | ✅ |

### 🐛 The classic case: an `if` with no `else`

```
if temperature > 30:
    raise_warning()
return status
```
A single test with `temperature = 35`:
- Every executable statement ran → **statement coverage 100%** ✅
- The FALSE outcome of the decision was never taken → **branch coverage 50%** ⚠️

> ⚠️ The absence of an `else` does **not** mean the FALSE branch does not exist. It exists, it is just empty, and it still has to be exercised.

---

## 6️⃣ What Branch Coverage Cannot Find

- ❌ Defects that require a specific **path** through the code
- ❌ Data-dependent defects
- ❌ Requirements that were never implemented (defects of omission)

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What is a branch?** | A transfer of control between two nodes (an arrow in the graph) |
| **Coverage item** | Branches |
| **Formula** | BCov = (branches exercised / total branches) × 100% |
| **How to count on a graph?** | Count the edges (arrows) |
| **How many branches per `if`?** | 2 (TRUE and FALSE) |
| **Subsumption?** | Branch coverage **subsumes** statement coverage, not vice versa |
4.3.3:
## 1️⃣ The Value in One Sentence

> **The strength of white-box testing: the ENTIRE implementation is taken into account.**
> It makes defect detection possible even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete — because the source is **the code itself, not a document**.

---

## 2️⃣ Strengths ✅

| Strength | Explanation | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 🔍 **The whole implementation is visible** | Even a badly written specification does not block you | The requirement has not been updated in 3 years, the code has 5 new conditions → white-box sees them |
| 📏 **Objective coverage measurement** | Answers "how much did I test?" with a **number** | "Branch coverage is 72%" |
| ➕ **Shows what is missing** | Lists uncovered branches → new tests get written | "Branch N4→N6 was never exercised" → add a test |
| 🤝 **Confidence in the code** | As coverage rises, confidence rises measurably | Hard evidence for a release decision |
| 📄 **Usable in static testing** | Applies even **without executing** the code | Dry runs, pseudocode, reviewing code not yet ready to run |

---

## 3️⃣ The Weakness ❌

> **It cannot find a requirement that was never implemented!**

```
Requirement : "Lock the account after 3 wrong password attempts"
Code        : The locking logic WAS NEVER WRITTEN

White-box testing → covers 100% of the code that exists ✅
                  → cannot test code that does not exist ❌
→ THE DEFECT OF OMISSION IS MISSED
```

> 🔑 White-box checks **what was written**, black-box checks **what should have been written**. That is why they are used together.

---

## 4️⃣ What You Lose With Black-Box Only

| | **Black-box only** | **Black-box + White-box** |
|---|---|---|
| Shows the requirements are met | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Measures actual code coverage** | ❌ **No** | ✅ Yes |
| Finds code that never runs | ❌ | ✅ |
| Finds a missing requirement | ✅ | ✅ |

> 🔑 **Performing only black-box testing does NOT provide a measure of actual code coverage.** Your 100 requirement-derived tests may never touch 40% of the code — and you would never know.

---

## 5️⃣ How the Two Complement Each Other

```
Black-box tests executed
      ↓
White-box tool measures coverage → branch coverage 68%
      ↓
Uncovered branches listed
      ↓
ADDITIONAL tests written for those branches
      ↓
Coverage rises to 95% → confidence in the code increases ✅
```

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Topic | White-box testing |
|---|---|
| **Core strength** | The entire implementation is taken into account |
| **If the specification is poor?** | Still works — the code is the source |
| **Core weakness** | Cannot detect defects of omission (unimplemented requirements) |
| **Usable in static testing?** | ✅ Yes (dry runs, pseudocode, code not ready to run) |
| **Does black-box measure coverage?** | ❌ No, it gives no measure of actual code coverage |
| **Benefit of coverage measures** | An objective number + tests to close the gaps + confidence |

|---|---|
| **Effectiveness depends on?** | Entirely on the **tester's skill** |
| **Their role?** | **Complementary** to black-box and white-box (not a replacement) |
| **What they find?** | Defects the formal techniques **miss** |
4.4.1:
## 1️⃣ The Reasoning Behind It

> **Error guessing** is the tester **anticipating**, from **their own knowledge**, where errors, defects and failures will show up.

The tester draws on three sources:

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| 📜 **How the application has worked in the past** | "Last release the invoice doubled at the midnight rollover" |
| 👨‍💻 **The kinds of errors these developers tend to make** | "This team keeps writing `>` where `>=` belongs" |
| 🔁 **Failures seen in other, similar applications** | "Every parking system struggles with a zero-minute stay" |

> 🔑 **What is anticipated: WHERE a defect might be.** Not its root cause, not its exact location — only its **likely places**.

---

## 2️⃣ Where Defects Live (6 categories — memorize)

| Category | Typical defects |
|---|---|
| ⌨️ **Input** | Correct input not accepted, wrong input accepted, parameters wrong or missing |
| 🖨️ **Output** | Wrong format, wrong result |
| 🧠 **Logic** | Missing cases, wrong operator |
| 🔢 **Computation** | Incorrect operand, wrong computation, division by zero |
| 🔌 **Interfaces** | Parameter mismatch, incompatible types |
| 🗃️ **Data** | Incorrect initialization, wrong type |

---

## 3️⃣ Fault Attacks

> **A fault attack is the METHODICAL way to implement error guessing.** Not loose intuition — a systematic list.

### Steps
```
1. Create or acquire a LIST of possible errors, defects and failures
        ↓
2. Design a test for each item that will EXPOSE that defect
        ↓
3. Execute the tests → trigger the defect
```

What is the list based on? → **Experience**, **defect and failure data**, or **common knowledge about why software fails**.

---

## 4️⃣ Worked Example — Parking Fee System 🅿️

Thinking about past projects and the developers' habits, the tester writes this list:

| # | Anticipated risky situation | Category |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Entry and exit happen in **the same minute** | Computation |
| 2 | The car is parked **across midnight** | Logic |
| 3 | The fee calculation runs for **0 minutes** | Computation |
| 4 | The plate field is submitted **empty** | Input |
| 5 | The fee comes out **negative** — what shows on screen? | Output |

The tester then derives **one test case per list item**.

> 🔑 This is **error guessing**: the tests come not from the specification but from **the defect list in the tester's head**.

---

## 5️⃣ Exam Distinctions

### ✅ This IS error guessing
- Building a list of likely defects from past failures
- Deriving tests from a list like "division by zero, wrong output format, correct input not accepted"
- Writing tests that target the developers' typical mistakes

### ❌ This is NOT error guessing
- Deriving partitions from ranges in the requirement → **Equivalence partitioning**
- Measuring branch coverage of the source code → **Branch testing**
- Working through the company's standard list → **Checklist-based testing**
- Finding the **root cause** of a defect → **Root cause analysis / debugging**

---

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Based on?** | The tester's knowledge: past behavior, developer habits, similar applications |
| **Its methodical form?** | Fault attacks |
| **Its output?** | A list of possible errors, defects and failures + tests that trigger them |
| **The 6 categories** | Input, output, logic, computation, interfaces, data |
| **What CANNOT be anticipated?** | The root cause and the exact location of a defect |
4.4.2:
## 1️⃣ The Essence of Exploratory Testing

> **Tests are designed, executed and evaluated SIMULTANEOUSLY while the tester learns about the test object.**

Conventional testing goes:
```
Design  →  Execute  →  Evaluate      (separate steps, separate times)
```
Exploratory testing:
```
Design + Execute + Evaluate + Learn   (all AT ONCE)
         ↓
What you learn decides the next test
```

The aim: **learn more** about the test object, **explore it deeply** with focused tests, and **create tests for untested areas**.

---

## 2️⃣ Session-Based Testing

This is the structure that makes exploratory testing **systematic and manageable**.

| Element | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ⏱️ **Time box** | The session is confined to a fixed duration | "90 minutes" |
| 📜 **Test charter** | Holds the test objectives and guides the session | "Explore the report filters, focus on date-range behavior" |
| 📝 **Test session sheet** | Documents the steps followed and discoveries made | "Entered 31 February → the app freezes" |
| 🗣️ **Debriefing** | After the session, tester and stakeholders discuss the results | A 15-minute review meeting |

> 🔑 **Test objectives = high-level test conditions.** Coverage items are not fixed up front — they are **identified and exercised during the session**.

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example — Energy Consumption Reporting Tool ⚡

Documentation is thin and time is short, so the tester runs a session-based exploratory session:

```
TEST CHARTER
Objective : Explore date-range selection and report generation
Time box  : 90 minutes
Tooling   : Browser + screen recording

SESSION SHEET
00:05  Normal range (1–31 Jan) → report generated ✅
00:18  End date < start date → no error message, empty report 🐛
00:31  400-day range → the 366-day rule was not applied 🐛
00:47  Range with no measurements → showed 0 kWh instead of "no data" 🐛
01:10  New idea: month-end / year-end rollover → separate session tomorrow

DEBRIEFING
3 defects found, 1 new test area identified, 2 questions raised with the business analyst
```

> 🔑 Every finding produced **the next test**. There was no pre-written list of test cases.

---

## 4️⃣ When to Use It

### ✅ Exploratory testing is useful when
- 📄 **Specifications are few or inadequate**
- ⏰ There is **significant time pressure** on the testing
- ➕ You want to **complement** other, **more formal** techniques
- 🧠 The tester is **experienced**, has **domain knowledge**, and shows **analytical skills, curiosity and creativity**

### ⚠️ Watch out
- Effectiveness depends **entirely on the tester's skill**
- It does **not replace** formal techniques, it complements them
- It **can incorporate other techniques** inside it (e.g. equivalence partitioning)

---

| **How it is structured** | Session-based testing |
| **Guiding document** | Test charter |
| **End of the session** | Debriefing |
| **When are coverage items identified?** | **During the session** |
| **When is it suitable?** | Inadequate specifications or time pressure |

4.4.3:
## 1️⃣ What Is It?

> The tester designs, implements and executes tests to **cover the test conditions on a checklist**.

Checklists are built from:
- 🧠 **Experience**
- 👤 **Knowledge of what matters to the user**
- 💥 **An understanding of why and how software fails**

---

## 2️⃣ What Makes a Good Checklist Item?

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ❓ **Phrased as a question** | "Does the form warn the user when submitted empty?" |
| 🔍 **Checkable separately** | Each item can be verified on its own |
| 🎯 **Checkable directly** | No room for interpretation |
| 🧩 **May refer to** | Requirements, graphical interface properties, quality characteristics, other test conditions |

### ❌ What should NOT be on a checklist
- 🤖 Items that can be **checked automatically** (a tool already does it)
- 🚦 Items better suited as **entry or exit criteria**
- ☁️ Items that are **too general** ("Is the application of good quality?")

---

## 3️⃣ Worked Example — Usability Checklist 📋

> 💡 Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are the best-known checklist example.

A pre-release review of an energy reporting tool:

| # | Checklist item | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does every screen show the user what the system is doing? | ✅ |
| 2 | Do error messages state the problem and the fix clearly? | ❌ |
| 3 | Can the user cancel an action started by mistake? | ✅ |
| 4 | Do report headings fit without overflowing in all languages? | ❌ |
| 5 | Is a meaningful message shown when there is no data? | ✅ |

> 🔑 Checklists support both **functional** and **non-functional** testing.

---

## 4️⃣ 🚨 Two Points the Exam Loves

### ⚠️ Point 1: Checklists GO BLUNT over time
```
The same list is used every release
       ↓
Developers LEARN to avoid those errors
       ↓
The list finds fewer and fewer defects 📉
       ↓
FIX: Update the checklist REGULARLY based on defect analysis
     (add entries for newly found high-severity defects)
       ↓
BUT: do not let the list grow too LONG!
```

### ⚠️ Point 2: Greater coverage, lower repeatability

| | Detailed test case | High-level checklist |
|---|---|---|
| **Steps** | Fully written out | General, open to interpretation |
| **Will two testers do the same thing?** | ✅ Yes | ❌ No, they take different paths |
| **Repeatability** | **High** | **Low** |
| **Coverage** | Narrow but exact | **Potentially greater** |

> 🔑 **Because checklists are high-level, variability occurs in the actual testing → potentially GREATER coverage but LESS repeatability.** The exam quotes this sentence almost verbatim.

---

## 5️⃣ When to Use It

- 📄 **When there are no detailed test cases** → the checklist provides **guidelines** and **some degree of consistency**
- 🔁 For **pre-release reviews** repeated every release
- 🎨 For **non-functional** testing (usability, accessibility)

---

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What is covered** | The test conditions on the checklist |
| **Item format** | Usually a **question** |
| **Must not be on the list** | Automatically checkable items, entry/exit criteria, overly general items |
| **What happens over time?** | It becomes less effective → update it from defect analysis |
| **List length** | Must not get too long |
| **Side effect** | Greater coverage ⬆️, lower repeatability ⬇️ |

## 🤝 What Is in This Section?

Every technique so far (4.2, 4.3, 4.4) aimed at **DETECTING** defects. Collaboration-based approaches aim at **AVOIDING** them.

| | **Test techniques (4.2 – 4.4)** | **Collaboration-based approaches (4.5)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | **Find** a defect that exists (defect detection) | Make sure the defect **never happens** (defect avoidance) |
| **Means** | Techniques, formulas, coverage | **Collaboration and communication** |
| **When?** | After the code or document exists | **Before** it is written, while talking |

Three topics:
- 📝 **Collaborative user story writing** (4.5.1)
- ✅ **Acceptance criteria** (4.5.2)
- 🔄 **Acceptance test-driven development — ATDD** (4.5.3)

> 🔑 Preventing a misunderstanding **by talking** is cheaper than finding the defect **by testing**.
4.5.1:
## 1️⃣ What Is a User Story?

> A user story represents **a feature that will be valuable to a user or purchaser** of the system.

### 📐 The most common format

```
As a [role],
I want [goal to be accomplished],
so that I can [resulting business value for the role]
```
…followed by the **acceptance criteria**.

> 💡 Example: "**As a member**, **I want** to freeze my membership from the app, **so that I** do not pay dues while on holiday."

---

## 2️⃣ 🚨 The 3 C's — Three Critical Aspects

| C | Aspect | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C** | **Card** | The **medium describing** the story | An index card, a Jira ticket, an entry on an electronic board |
| **C** | **Conversation** | Explains **how the software will be used** — may be **verbal or documented** | A workshop between the business representative, developer and tester |
| **C** | **Confirmation** | The **acceptance criteria** (see 4.5.2) | "A freeze can last at most 90 days" |

> 🔑 **Confirmation = acceptance criteria.** The exam asks for exactly this mapping.
> 🔑 Card is the **medium** (where it is written), Conversation is the **understanding** (how it will be used), Confirmation is the **condition** (when it counts as done).

---

## 3️⃣ Why Collaboration Matters — Three Perspectives

Collaborative authorship gives the team a **SHARED VISION of what should be delivered**. Three perspectives sit at the table:

| Perspective | Its question |
|---|---|
| 💼 **Business** | What value does this feature give the user? |
| 👨‍💻 **Development** | How do we build it, how long will it take? |
| 🧪 **Testing** | How do we test it, where will it break? |

Techniques that help: **brainstorming**, **mind mapping**.

> 🔑 The MOST important benefit of collaboration: **shared understanding** → defects caused by misunderstanding are prevented **before anything is written**.

---

## 4️⃣ INVEST — Six Properties of a Good Story

| Letter | Property | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | **Independent** | Can be built without depending on another story |
| **N** | **Negotiable** | The details can change through discussion |
| **V** | **Valuable** | Delivers real benefit to the user |
| **E** | **Estimable** | The effort can be estimated |
| **S** | **Small** | Fits inside one sprint |
| **T** | **Testable** | It is clear how it will be verified |

---

## 5️⃣ What If Someone Says "I Do Not Know How to Test It"?

If a stakeholder does not know how to test the story, it points to **one of three things**:

```
1️⃣ The story is NOT CLEAR ENOUGH
2️⃣ The story does NOT REFLECT SOMETHING VALUABLE to them
3️⃣ The stakeholder simply NEEDS HELP with testing
```

> 🔑 A story that cannot be tested is usually a **badly written** story.

---

| Concept | In short |
|---|---|
| **User story** | A feature valuable to a user or purchaser |
| **Format** | As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [business value] |
| **Card** | The medium describing the story |

| **Confirmation** | The acceptance criteria |
| **Three perspectives** | Business, development, testing |
| **INVEST** | Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable |

4.5.2:
## 1️⃣ What Are Acceptance Criteria?

> The **conditions** an implementation of a user story must meet **to be accepted by stakeholders**.

### 🔑 What they mean to a tester

```
Acceptance criteria  =  TEST CONDITIONS
                        (the conditions the tests should exercise)
```

Where do they come from? → Usually a result of the **Conversation** (see 4.5.1 — the **Confirmation** leg of the 3 C's).

---

## 2️⃣ What Acceptance Criteria Are Used For (5 purposes)

| # | Purpose | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| 1️⃣ | **Define the scope of the story** | Say where the story begins and ends |
| 2️⃣ | **Reach consensus among stakeholders** | Everyone agrees on the definition of done |
| 3️⃣ | **Describe both positive AND negative scenarios** | Not only the happy path, error cases too |
| 4️⃣ | **Serve as a basis for acceptance testing** | They are the input to ATDD (see 4.5.3) |
| 5️⃣ | **Allow accurate planning and estimation** | A clear scope makes effort estimates reliable |

---

## 3️⃣ 🚨 The Two Formats

### 📜 A) Scenario-oriented

**Given / When / Then** — the format used in BDD (see section 2.1.3).

```
AC-A:
Given : the member has no outstanding dues
When  : the member scans their card at the turnstile
Then  : the turnstile opens and the entry is logged
```

> 🔑 **What distinguishes it:** each criterion describes **one concrete scenario** as a **precondition → action → expected result** triple.

### 📋 B) Rule-oriented

A **bullet point verification list** or a **tabulated input-output mapping**.

```
AC-B:
• A membership freeze lasts at most 90 days
• A freeze can only be started for an active membership
• No dues are charged during the frozen period
```

Or as a table:

| Input: freeze duration | Expected output |
|---|---|
| 1 – 90 days | Freeze starts ✅ |
| 0 days | "Invalid duration" error ❌ |
| 91 days | "90 days maximum" error ❌ |

> 🔑 **What distinguishes it:** a **list of rules**, not a scenario. It states **conditions**, not a flow.

---

## 4️⃣ The Two Formats Side by Side

| | **Scenario-oriented** | **Rule-oriented** |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape** | Given / When / Then | Bullet list or input-output table |
| **Comes from** | BDD | Classic requirement writing |
| **Describes** | A concrete **flow** | The applicable **rules** |
| **Fit for automation** | Very high (Cucumber, SpecFlow) | Medium |

> ⚠️ Most acceptance criteria fit **one** of these two formats. But the team may use **its own custom format**, as long as the criteria are **well-defined and unambiguous**.

---

## 5️⃣ What a Good Scenario-Oriented Criterion Looks Like

### ✅ Correct
```
Given : the homeowner has "holiday mode" on and the time is 19:00
When  : the controller triggers the evening lighting
Then  : the living room lamp switches on at a random minute between 19:00 and 19:30
```

### ❌ Wrong
```
"Lighting should work properly"      → too general, not measurable
"The system should be fast"          → no concrete threshold
"Given the user logs in"             → an action written as a precondition
```

---

| **Format 1** | Scenario-oriented → Given / When / Then (BDD) |
| **Format 2** | Rule-oriented → bullet list or input-output table |
| **Any other format?** | ✅ Yes, as long as it is well-defined and unambiguous |
4.5.3:
## 1️⃣ What Is ATDD?

> **ATDD (Acceptance Test-Driven Development)** is a **test-first** approach.

```
BEFORE the user story is implemented
         ↓
The test cases are created
         ↓
Then the code is written
```

The test cases are created by **team members with different perspectives**: **customer + developer + tester**. They may be executed **manually or automated**.

---

## 2️⃣ ATDD Step by Step

```
1️⃣ SPECIFICATION WORKSHOP
   The team analyzes, discusses and writes the user story
   and (if not yet defined) its acceptance criteria
   → Incompleteness, ambiguities and defects are resolved HERE
        ↓
2️⃣ TEST CASES ARE CREATED
   By the team as a whole, or by the tester individually
   The cases are based on the ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
   → They read like EXAMPLES of how the software works
        ↓
3️⃣ THE DEVELOPER WRITES THE CODE
   Guided by the tests, implementing the story correctly
        ↓
4️⃣ THE TESTS ARE AUTOMATED (if the format supports it)
   → Acceptance tests become EXECUTABLE REQUIREMENTS
```

> 🔑 **An example IS a test.** In ATDD the two terms are used interchangeably.

---

## 3️⃣ 🚨 The Order of Test Cases (the exam asks)

```
1. POSITIVE tests      → No exceptions or errors, everything as expected
         ↓
2. NEGATIVE tests      → Error conditions, invalid inputs
         ↓
3. NON-FUNCTIONAL      → Performance efficiency, usability, etc.
```

> 🔑 Happy path first, then the error paths, then the quality characteristics.

---

## 4️⃣ Rules for the Test Cases

### ✅ They must
- 🗣️ Be expressed so that **stakeholders understand them**
- 📝 Use **natural language** sentences: **preconditions** (if any) + **inputs** + **postconditions**
- 🎯 Cover **all the characteristics** of the user story
- 🔧 Use the **test techniques** from 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4 during design

### ❌ They must not
- ❌ **Go beyond the story**
- ❌ Have **two test cases describing the same characteristic** (no duplicates)

> ⚠️ However, the **acceptance criteria may detail** some of the issues mentioned in the story — that is not going beyond scope.

---

## 5️⃣ Worked Example — EV Charging Station ⚡

**User story:** "As a driver, I want to start a charging session from the mobile app."

**Acceptance criteria:**
| # | Criterion |
|---|---|
| **AC1** | Balance ≥ 50 **and** the socket is free → the session starts |
| **AC2** | Balance < 50 → no session, "Insufficient balance" warning |
| **AC3** | The socket is not free → no session, "Socket busy" warning |

### Test cases derived with ATDD

| TC | Type | Precondition | Input / Action | Postcondition (expected) | Criterion |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TC1** | ✅ Positive | Balance 120, socket free | Start charging | Session started | AC1 |
| **TC2** | ✅ Positive | Balance **exactly 50**, socket free | Start charging | Session started (boundary!) | AC1 |
| **TC3** | ❌ Negative | Balance 49, socket free | Start charging | "Insufficient balance", no session | AC2 |
| **TC4** | ❌ Negative | Balance 120, socket **occupied** | Start charging | "Socket busy", no session | AC3 |
| **TC5** | ⚡ Non-functional | Balance 120, socket free | Start charging | Session starts in **under 3 seconds** | — |

> 💡 **Note TC2:** **boundary value analysis** was applied during design (50 and 49). ATDD does not prevent you from using the techniques in 4.2–4.4, it **encourages** it.
> ⚠️ **TC1 and TC2 do not describe the same characteristic** — one is a typical value, one is a boundary. What is forbidden is writing the **identical** characteristic twice.

---

## 6️⃣ Executable Requirements

```
Test cases captured in a format a test automation
framework supports (e.g. Gherkin)
         ↓
The developer writes the supporting code while
implementing the feature
         ↓
Acceptance tests = EXECUTABLE REQUIREMENTS
         ↓
The specification becomes living and automatically verified
```

---

5.1.1:
## 1️⃣ What Is a Test Plan?

A **test plan** is the document that states the **objectives, resources and processes** of a test project.

> 💡 Example: a plan for a **hotel booking system** → "Booking, cancellation and payment flows will be tested for 3 weeks with 4 testers."

---

## 2️⃣ What Is a Test Plan For? (4 Purposes)

| Purpose | What it means |
|---|---|
| 📄 **It documents** | Writes down the means and the schedule for achieving the test objectives |
| ✅ **It secures criteria** | Helps the performed test activities meet the established criteria |
| 🗣️ **It is a communication tool** | Creates a shared language with team members and stakeholders |
| 🧭 **It shows conformance** | Shows the test process conforms to the test policy and test strategy — or explains **why it does not** |

Writing the plan is valuable in itself: it forces the tester to think ahead about **risks, schedules, people, tools, costs and effort**.

---

## 3️⃣ Typical Test Plan Content

| # | Content | Example (hotel booking) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Test context** (scope, test objectives, test basis) | "Scope: booking + payment; basis: user stories" |
| 2 | **Assumptions and constraints** | "The payment provider's simulator will be available" |
| 3 | **Stakeholders** (roles, responsibilities, relevance to testing, hiring and training needs) | "2 senior + 2 junior; API training for the juniors" |
| 4 | **Communication** (form, frequency, documentation templates) | "Weekly status mail, Jira template" |
| 5 | **Risk register** (product risks + project risks) | "Double-booking risk: high" |
| 6 | **Test approach** | Test levels, test types, test techniques, test deliverables, **entry and exit criteria**, independence of testing, metrics to be collected, test data and test environment requirements, deviations from the test policy and strategy |
| 7 | **Budget and schedule** | "$40,000, 3 weeks" |

> 📚 More detail: the **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3** standard.

---

## ❌ These Are NOT Expected In a Test Plan

- 🐛 **Individual defect reports** → these appear during execution, not in the plan
- 📊 **Actual test results / execution logs** → that is the test completion report's job
- 🧾 **Test summary and lessons learned** → written **after** testing ends
- 🔍 **Root cause analysis** → part of defect management
- 💻 **The source code or detailed design** → that is development's job

> 🔑 A test plan **plans the future**; a test completion report **describes the past**

---

| Question | Answer in the test plan |

| What will we test? | Test context, scope, test basis |
| Who will test? | Stakeholders, roles, training needs |
| How will we test? | Test approach (levels, types, techniques) |
| When does it start/end? | Entry and exit criteria, schedule |
| What are we accepting? | Risk register, assumptions, constraints |
| What will it cost? | Budget |

## 1️⃣ Iterative SDLCs Have Two Kinds of Planning

| | **Release Planning** | **Iteration Planning** |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizon** | Looks ahead to the **release of the product** (many iterations) | Looks ahead to the end of **a single iteration** |
| **Backlog** | The **product backlog** is defined and re-defined | The **iteration backlog** |
| **User stories** | Larger stories are refined into sets of smaller stories | Stories are broken down into **tasks** |
| **Role** | The **basis for the test approach and test plan** across all iterations | The detailed plan for that one iteration |

---

## 2️⃣ What the Tester Does in Release Planning

- ✍️ Participates in writing **testable user stories and acceptance criteria**
- ⚠️ Participates in **project and quality risk analyses**
- 🧮 **Estimates the test effort** associated with user stories
- 🧭 **Determines the test approach**
- 📄 **Plans the testing** for the release

> 💡 Example — e-commerce cart: getting "cannot be added when stock is 0" added as an acceptance criterion to the story "user adds a product to the cart" → a release planning contribution.

---

## 3️⃣ What the Tester Does in Iteration Planning

- 🔍 Participates in the **detailed risk analysis of user stories**
- 🧪 **Determines the testability** of user stories
- 🧱 **Breaks user stories down into tasks** (particularly **testing tasks**)
- ⏱️ **Estimates test effort for all testing tasks**
- 🧩 **Identifies and refines the functional and non-functional aspects** of the test object

> 💡 Example — e-commerce cart: splitting "add to cart" into "write the API test / run on Chrome + Safari / prepare stock data" → an iteration planning contribution.

---

## ❌ These Are NOT the Tester's Planning Contributions

- ❌ Writing production code / fixing the defect → the **developer's** job
- ❌ Making the **final call on backlog priority** → the **product owner's** job
- ❌ Setting the release date single-handedly
- ❌ Removing the root cause of found defects → that is **debugging**

---

| Contribution | Release Planning | Iteration Planning |
|---|---|---|
| Writing testable stories + acceptance criteria | ✅ | — |
| Project and quality risk analysis | ✅ (overall) | ✅ (detailed, per story) |
| Test effort estimation | ✅ (per story) | ✅ (for all testing tasks) |
| Determining the test approach | ✅ | — |
| Determining story testability | — | ✅ |
| Breaking stories into testing tasks | — | ✅ |
| Refining functional/non-functional aspects | — | ✅ |

> 🔑 **Release** → the big picture and the approach; **Iteration** → the detail, the tasks and testability

## 1️⃣ Two Gates: Entry and Exit

| | **Entry Criteria** | **Exit Criteria** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | The preconditions for **starting** a given activity | What must be achieved to **declare an activity completed** |
| **Question** | "Are we ready to start?" | "Can we call this done?" |
| **If not met** | The activity becomes **more difficult, time-consuming, costly and riskier** | Testing is not finished |
| **Agile name** | **Definition of Ready** | **Definition of Done** |

> 🔑 Entry criteria → **the condition to walk in**; exit criteria → **the condition to walk out**

They should be defined for **each test level** and differ **based on the test objectives**.

---

## 2️⃣ Typical Entry Criteria (3 Groups)

| Group | Example |
|---|---|
| 🧰 **Availability of resources** | People, tools, environments, test data, budget, time |
| 📄 **Availability of testware** | Test basis, testable requirements, user stories, test cases |
| 🚦 **Initial quality level of the test object** | **All smoke tests have passed**, the code compiles |

> 💡 DevOps example: the entry criterion for the step "commit the code to version control and merge into the **test** branch" → **the code has passed static analysis / code review and builds successfully**.

---

## 3️⃣ Typical Exit Criteria (2 Groups)

| Group | Example |
|---|---|
| 📏 **Measures of thoroughness** (numeric) | Achieved level of coverage (e.g., 90% statement coverage), number of unresolved defects, defect density, number of failed test cases |
| ✅❌ **Binary "yes/no" criteria** | Planned tests have been executed, static testing has been performed, all defects found are reported, all regression tests are automated |

---

## 4️⃣ Exam Trap: Running Out of Time or Money

- ⏳ **Running out of time or budget is also a valid exit criterion!**
- Even when other exit criteria are not satisfied, ending testing is acceptable **if the stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk** of going live.

---

## ✅ These Are Exit Criteria
- "All critical and high-priority defects are closed"
- "Requirements coverage has reached 100%"
- "All 320 planned test cases have been executed"
- "The test budget is spent and stakeholders accepted the risk"

## ❌ These Are NOT Exit Criteria (They Are Entry Criteria)
- "The test environment is installed and verified"
- "Test data has been prepared"
- "Smoke tests have passed"
- "Requirements have been made testable"

---

5.1.4:
## 1️⃣ What Is Test Effort Estimation?

**Test effort estimation** means predicting the **amount of test-related work** needed to meet the test objectives.

- ⚠️ An estimate rests on **assumptions** and is **always subject to estimation error** → say so clearly to stakeholders
- 🔬 **Estimation for small tasks is more accurate than for large ones**
- 🧱 So a large task is **decomposed into smaller tasks**, each estimated separately

---

## 2️⃣ Four Techniques — Which Is Which?

| Technique | Type | Based on | In one line |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Estimation based on ratios** | 📊 Metrics-based | Data from **previous projects** | "The ratio was 3:2 before, it will be again" |
| **Extrapolation** | 📊 Metrics-based | **Early measurements in the current project** | "Look at the last 3 iterations, project the next one" |
| **Wideband Delphi** | 👤 Expert-based | **Iterative** expert estimates | "Everyone estimates alone, discusses, repeats → consensus" |
| **Three-point estimation** | 👤 Expert-based | Three estimates **a, m, b** | "Optimistic + 4×likely + pessimistic, divide by 6" |

> 🔑 **Historical data** → metrics-based; **human judgement** → expert-based

---

## 3️⃣ 📊 Estimation Based on Ratios

Figures are collected from the organization's **previous projects** → **"standard" ratios** are derived for similar projects. The best source is **the organization's own historical data**.

> 💡 **Worked example:**
> ```
> Previous project development : test ratio = 3 : 2
> New project development effort = 600 person-days
> → Test effort = 600 × (2/3) = 400 person-days
> ```

---

## 4️⃣ 📊 Extrapolation

Measurements are taken **as early as possible** in the current project; once there are enough observations, the remaining work is approximated with a **mathematical model**. **Very suitable for iterative SDLCs.**

> 💡 **Worked example — model:** `E(n) = (3 × A(n-1) + A(n-2)) / 4`
> ```
> A(1) = 20 person-days (actual in iteration 1)
> A(2) = 24 person-days (actual in iteration 2)
> E(3) = (3 × 24 + 20) / 4 = (72 + 20) / 4 = 23 person-days
> ```
> A simpler variant: "effort for the next iteration = the average of the last three iterations"

---

## 5️⃣ 👤 Wideband Delphi

```
Each expert estimates IN ISOLATION
    ↓
Estimates are collected
    ↓
If deviations fall outside the agreed boundaries → the experts DISCUSS
    ↓
Everyone estimates AGAIN, IN ISOLATION
    ↓
Repeat until CONSENSUS is reached
```

- 🃏 **Planning Poker** = the **variant** of Wideband Delphi commonly used in Agile; estimates are made with **cards carrying numbers** that represent the effort size.

---

## 6️⃣ 👤 Three-Point Estimation (The Exam's Favourite)

The experts give three estimates:
- 🟢 **a** = most optimistic estimation
- 🟡 **m** = most likely estimation
- 🔴 **b** = most pessimistic estimation

```
E  = (a + 4m + b) / 6      ← weighted arithmetic mean
SD = (b − a) / 6           ← measurement error (standard deviation)
```

> 💡 **Syllabus example:** a=6, m=9, b=18
> ```
> E  = (6 + 36 + 18) / 6 = 10
> SD = (18 − 6) / 6 = 2
> → 10 ± 2 person-hours (i.e., between 8 and 12)
> ```

### 🧮 Practice Table

| a | m | b | E = (a+4m+b)/6 | SD = (b−a)/6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 11 | 14 | (2+44+14)/6 = **10** | 2 |
| 8 | 14 | 26 | (8+56+26)/6 = **15** | **3** → 15±3 |
| 8 | 14 | 32 | (8+56+32)/6 = **16** | 4 |
| 8 | 20 | 26 | (8+80+26)/6 = **19** | 3 |
| 9 | 14 | 25 | (9+56+25)/6 = **15** | ~2.67 |
| 1 | 3 | 8 | (1+12+8)/6 = **3.5** (one case) → **4 cases = 14 hours** | ~1.17 |

> ⚠️ If the question says "4 test cases": first find E for **one** case, then **multiply by 4**.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Technique | Type | Keyword |
|---|---|---|
| **Based on ratios** | Metrics-based | Previous projects, 3:2 ratio |
| **Extrapolation** | Metrics-based | Recent iterations of the current project |
| **Wideband Delphi** | Expert-based | Isolated estimates + discussion + consensus, Planning Poker |
| **Three-point** | Expert-based | E=(a+4m+b)/6, SD=(b−a)/6 |
5.1.5:
## 1️⃣ What Is a Test Execution Schedule?

Once test cases and test procedures are specified and assembled into **test suites**, those suites are arranged in a **test execution schedule** that defines **the order in which they run**.

---

## 2️⃣ Three Prioritization Strategies

| Strategy | Order based on | Executed first |
|---|---|---|
| ⚠️ **Risk-based** | The **results of risk analysis** | Test cases covering the **most important risks** |
| 📐 **Coverage-based** | Coverage (e.g., statement coverage) | Test cases achieving the **highest coverage** |
| 📋 **Requirements-based** | Requirement priorities defined by **stakeholders** | Test cases tied to the **most important requirements** |

### 📐 Special variant: Additional Coverage
The first test = the one with the **highest coverage**. Each subsequent test = the one achieving the **highest ADDITIONAL coverage** (the most items not yet covered).

> 💡 **Worked example — traceability matrix (X = covers):**
> ```
>      R1  R2  R3  R4  R5  R6  R7
> TC1   X       X   X           X     → 4 requirements
> TC2   X               X       X     → 3 requirements
> TC3                   X   X         → 2 requirements
> TC4       X                         → 1 requirement
> ```
> ```
> Step 1: Highest coverage → TC1 (4)        Covered: R1,R3,R4,R7
> Step 2: Additional → TC2:+R5(1)  TC3:+R5,R6(2)  TC4:+R2(1)  → TC3 wins
> Step 3: R2 remains → TC4 (+1), TC2 (+0)   → TC4
> Step 4: TC2
> ORDER: TC1 → TC3 → TC4 → TC2
> ```

---

## 3️⃣ ⚠️ Risk-Based Prioritization — A Real Calculation

**Risk level = Likelihood × Impact** → sort from highest to lowest.

> 💡 **Example — irrigation automation system (1–5 scale):**
>
> | Test case | Likelihood | Impact | Risk level |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | TC1 | 3 | 5 | **15** |
> | TC2 | 5 | 2 | **10** |
> | TC3 | 4 | 4 | **16** ⬅ highest |
> | TC4 | 2 | 3 | **6** |
>
> ```
> ORDER: TC3 (16) → TC1 (15) → TC2 (10) → TC4 (6)
> ```

> ⚠️ Careful: do not look at likelihood alone or impact alone — the **product** decides. TC2 has the highest likelihood (5) but comes third.

---

## 4️⃣ Two Things That Override Priority

### 🔗 1. Dependencies
> **If a higher-priority test case depends on a lower-priority one → the lower-priority test case runs FIRST.**

> 💡 Example — restaurant finder app:
> ```
> TC001 "Select cuisine type"  → Priority 3, no dependency
> TC002 "Select restaurant"    → Priority 2, depends on TC001
> → Even though TC002 ranks higher, TC001 must run first
> ```

### 🧰 2. Resource Availability
The required **test tools, test environments or people** may only be available for a specific time window → the schedule shifts around it.

> 💡 Example: the payment provider's test environment is only up on Tuesdays → payment tests move to Tuesday.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| Risk analysis exists | Likelihood × Impact → highest first |
| A code coverage target exists | Highest-coverage test first |
| The question says "additional coverage" | At each step, the most **newly** covered items |
| Stakeholders set requirement priorities | Test of the most important requirement first |
| A high-priority test depends on another | **The test it depends on goes first** |
| Tool/environment/people constrained | Adjust the schedule to availability |

> 🔑 **Priority sets the order; dependency breaks the order**
5.1.6:
## 1️⃣ What Is the Test Pyramid?

The **test pyramid** is a **model** showing that different tests may have **different granularity**.

It supports the team in two things:
- 🤖 **Test automation**
- ⚖️ **Test effort allocation**

because it shows that **different test objectives are supported by different levels of test automation.**

---

## 2️⃣ What Do the Layers Say?

```
          ▲  TOP LAYER
         ╱ ╲  End-to-end / UI tests
        ╱   ╲  • Complex, high-level
       ╱─────╲ • SLOW, LOW isolation, LOW granularity
      ╱       ╲ • Large piece of functionality → only a FEW needed
     ╱ Service ╲
    ╱Integration╲
   ╱─────────────╲
  ╱ Unit/Component╲ • Small, isolated, FAST
 ╱     tests       ╲ • Small piece of functionality
╱───────────────────╲ • MANY needed for reasonable coverage
        BOTTOM LAYER
```

| As the layer gets higher | What happens? |
|---|---|
| **Test granularity** | 🔻 Decreases |
| **Test isolation** (degree of dependency on other system elements) | 🔻 Decreases |
| **Test execution time** | 🔺 Increases |
| **Number of tests needed** | 🔻 Decreases |

---

## 3️⃣ Layer Names Can Differ

| Model | Layers |
|---|---|
| **Original model (Cohn 2009)** | Unit tests → **Service tests** → **UI tests** |
| **Another popular model** | Unit (component) → Integration (component integration) → **End-to-end** |

> ℹ️ The **number and naming of the layers may differ**; other test levels can also be used.

---

## ✅ TRUE Statements About the Pyramid
- Bottom-layer tests are **small, isolated and fast**, and **many** are needed for reasonable coverage
- Top-layer tests are **slower**, check a large piece of functionality, and **just a few** suffice
- The model helps the team with **test automation and effort allocation**
- **Going up: granularity and isolation drop, execution time rises**

## ❌ FALSE Statements About the Pyramid
- ❌ "Tests get more granular as you go up" → the opposite
- ❌ "There should be more tests in the top layer" → the opposite, only a few
- ❌ "The pyramid replaces test levels" → no, it is a **model**
- ❌ "The number and names of layers are fixed" → no, they vary
- ❌ "It only applies to manual testing" → no, it is especially about **automation**

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| | **Bottom layer** (unit/component) | **Top layer** (end-to-end/UI) |
|---|---|---|
| **Granularity** | High | Low |
| **Isolation** | High | Low |
| **Speed** | Fast | Slow |
| **Scope covered** | Small piece of functionality | Large piece of functionality |
| **Number needed** | Many | Few |

> 🔑 **Go down** → many, small, fast; **go up** → few, large, slow
5.1.7:
## 1️⃣ What Are the Testing Quadrants?

The **testing quadrants**, defined by Brian Marick (Marick 2003, Crispin 2008), group **test levels** with the appropriate **test types, activities, test techniques and work products** in Agile software development.

What they are good for:
- 👁️ They let test management **visualize** these, so all appropriate test types and levels are **included in the SDLC**
- 🧠 They show that some test types are **more relevant to certain test levels** than others
- 🗣️ They give all stakeholders — developers, testers and **business representatives** — a way to **differentiate and describe** test types

---

## 2️⃣ Two Axes → Four Quadrants

```
                 SUPPORT THE TEAM              CRITIQUE THE PRODUCT
              (guide the development)   (measure behavior vs expectations)
            ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
BUSINESS    │           Q2             │           Q3             │
FACING      ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
TECHNOLOGY  │           Q1             │           Q4             │
FACING      └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

| Quadrant | Two dimensions | Contents | Automation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Q1** | 💻 Technology facing + 🤝 Support the team | **Component tests**, **component integration tests** | **Should be automated and included in the CI process** |
| **Q2** | 💼 Business facing + 🤝 Support the team | **Functional tests**, examples, **user story tests**, user experience prototypes, **API testing**, simulations | Can be **manual or automated**; checks the **acceptance criteria** |
| **Q3** | 💼 Business facing + 🔍 Critique the product | **Exploratory testing**, **usability testing**, **user acceptance testing** | **User-oriented, often manual** |
| **Q4** | 💻 Technology facing + 🔍 Critique the product | **Smoke tests** and **non-functional tests** (except usability): performance, load, security, reliability, portability | **Often automated** |

---

## 3️⃣ The Mappings the Exam Asks For

| Test | Quadrant | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| **Component testing** | **Q1** | Technology facing, supports the team |
| **Functional testing** | **Q2** | Business facing, supports the team |
| **User story testing / API testing** | **Q2** | Checks acceptance criteria |
| **Usability testing** | **Q3** | Business facing, critiques the product (the one exception to Q4!) |
| **Exploratory / user acceptance testing** | **Q3** | User-oriented, manual |
| **Reliability testing** | **Q4** | Non-functional, technology facing |
| **Load / performance testing** (e.g., response time under 5000 concurrent calls) | **Q4** | Non-functional + automated |
| **Smoke testing** | **Q4** | Technology facing, critiques the product |

> ⚠️ **Trap:** usability testing is a non-functional test, but it sits in **Q3, not Q4.** Q4 says "except usability tests".

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| | **Support the team** | **Critique the product** |
|---|---|---|
| **Business facing** | **Q2** — functional tests, story tests, API, prototypes, simulations | **Q3** — exploratory, usability, user acceptance |
| **Technology facing** | **Q1** — component, component integration (automated in CI) | **Q4** — smoke + non-functional (except usability) |

> 🔑 **Left column** (Q1, Q2) → **guides** development; **right column** (Q3, Q4) → **measures/critiques** the product
> 🔑 **Bottom row** (Q1, Q4) → technology, mostly automated; **top row** (Q2, Q3) → business, Q3 mostly manual
