## 1️⃣ Why Risk Management?

Organizations face many **internal and external factors** that make it uncertain **whether and when** they will achieve their objectives (ISO 31000).

Risk management lets them:
- 🎯 **Increase the likelihood** of achieving objectives
- 💎 **Improve the quality** of their products
- 🤝 **Increase stakeholders' confidence and trust**

---

## 2️⃣ The Two Main Risk Management Activities

| Activity | Consists of | Section |
|---|---|---|
| 🔍 **Risk analysis** | **Risk identification** + **risk assessment** | 5.2.3 |
| 🛡️ **Risk control** | **Risk mitigation** + **risk monitoring** | 5.2.4 |

```
RISK MANAGEMENT
    │
    ├── RISK ANALYSIS
    │      ├── Risk identification → "Which risks exist?"
    │      └── Risk assessment     → "How serious? Likelihood × Impact"
    │
    └── RISK CONTROL
           ├── Risk mitigation → "How do we bring the risk down?"
           └── Risk monitoring → "Did our measures actually work?"
```

---

## 3️⃣ Risk-Based Testing

> **The test approach in which test activities are selected, prioritized and managed based on risk analysis and risk control is called risk-based testing.**

> 💡 Example — an **ATM application**: "the balance is deducted incorrectly on withdrawal" is the highest-level risk → most of the test effort goes there, while "receipt font" gets very little.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Concept | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Risk analysis** | **Find** the risks and **score** them |
| **Risk control** | **Act** on the risks and **track** the action |
| **Risk-based testing** | Select, prioritize and manage testing **by risk** |

> 🔑 **Analysis** → what we don't know; **Control** → what we do about it
5.2.1:
## 1️⃣ What Is a Risk?

> A **risk** is a potential **event, hazard, threat or situation** whose occurrence causes an **adverse effect.**

It has not happened yet — it **might** happen. (Once it happens it is no longer a risk; it is an **issue**.)

---

## 2️⃣ The Two Attributes of a Risk

| Attribute | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| 🎲 **Risk likelihood** | The **probability of the risk occurring** | **Greater than zero and less than one** (0 < p < 1) |
| 💥 **Risk impact (harm)** | The **consequences** of that occurrence | The size of the harm |

---

## 3️⃣ Risk Level = Likelihood × Impact

> These two factors together express the **risk level** — the **measure** of the risk.
> **The higher the risk level, the more important its treatment.**

```
Risk level = Risk likelihood × Risk impact
```

---

## 4️⃣ 🧮 Worked Calculations

> 💡 **Example 1 — solving backwards (this comes up in the exam):**
> ```
> Risk level  = $1,000
> Likelihood  = 50% = 0.5
> Impact      = ?
>
> 1,000 = 0.5 × Impact
> → Impact = 1,000 / 0.5 = $2,000
> ```

> 💡 **Example 2 — hotel booking system (1–5 scale):**
>
> | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Risk level |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | The same room is sold twice | 3 | 5 | **15** 🔴 |
> | The payment is charged twice | 2 | 5 | **10** 🟠 |
> | The confirmation email is late | 5 | 1 | **5** 🟡 |
> | The hotel photo looks blurry | 4 | 1 | **4** 🟢 |
>
> → The "same room sold twice" risk is treated first.

> ⚠️ **Trap:** the highest likelihood is NOT the highest risk. "Email is late" has the highest likelihood (5) but low impact → low risk level.

---

## 5️⃣ Two Approaches

| Approach | How the risk level is found |
|---|---|
| 🔢 **Quantitative** | The **multiplication** of likelihood and impact (a number) |
| 🎨 **Qualitative** | A **risk matrix** (low/medium/high) |

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Concept | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Risk** | A potential event that could cause an adverse effect |
| **Risk likelihood** | The probability it occurs (between 0 and 1) |
| **Risk impact** | How much harm it does if it occurs |
| **Risk level** | **Likelihood × Impact** — the measure of the risk |

> 🔑 **High risk level** → **treated first**, gets the most test effort
5.2.2:
## 1️⃣ Two Types of Risk

In software testing one is generally concerned with **two types of risk**:

| | **Project Risk** | **Product Risk** |
|---|---|---|
| **Related to** | The **management and control** of the project | The product's **quality characteristics** (ISO 25010) |
| **Its question** | "Can we **deliver the project**?" | "Will the **product** behave wrongly?" |
| **If it occurs, it hits** | Schedule, **budget**, scope | Users, customers, reputation, safety |
| **Who worries?** | The project manager | Users and the business |

> 🔑 **Project risk** → harms the project; **product risk** → harms the user

---

## 2️⃣ 📋 Project Risks — 4 Categories

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| 🏢 **Organizational issues** | **Delays in work product deliveries**, **inaccurate estimates**, cost cutting |
| 👥 **People issues** | **Insufficient skills**, conflicts, **communication problems**, **shortage of staff** |
| 🔧 **Technical issues** | **Scope creep**, **poor tool support** |
| 🚚 **Supplier issues** | **Third-party delivery failure**, **bankruptcy** of the supporting company |

> ➡️ When project risks occur they hit the project's **schedule, budget or scope**, which lowers its **ability to achieve its objectives**.

---

## 3️⃣ 🐛 Product Risks — Examples

- ❌ **Missing or wrong functionality**
- 🧮 **Incorrect calculations**
- 💥 **Runtime errors**
- 🏗️ **Poor architecture**
- 🐌 **Inefficient algorithms**, **inadequate response time**
- 😤 **Poor user experience**
- 🔓 **Security vulnerabilities**

### What happens when a product risk occurs?
- 😠 User dissatisfaction
- 💸 **Loss of revenue, trust, reputation**
- 🧍 **Damage to third parties**
- 🛠️ High maintenance costs, **overload of the help desk**
- ⚖️ **Criminal penalties**
- ☠️ In extreme cases, **physical damage, injuries or even death**

---

## 4️⃣ 🧪 Exam Practice — Which Is Which?

| Risk statement | Type |
|---|---|
| "The refund calculation returns the wrong amount" | 🐛 **Product** |
| "Delivery of the test environment slipped by 2 weeks" | 📋 **Project** |
| "Nobody on the team knows API automation" | 📋 **Project** |
| "Campaign coupons can be stacked on top of each other" | 🐛 **Product** |
| "The payment provider cancelled the contract" | 📋 **Project** (supplier) |
| "The page takes 30 seconds to load at 5000 users" | 🐛 **Product** |
| "Test effort was underestimated" | 📋 **Project** (organizational) |
| "User passwords are stored unencrypted" | 🐛 **Product** (security) |

> ⚠️ **Shortcut:** if the sentence mentions **people, schedule, budget, tools or suppliers** → **project risk.**
> If it describes **how the software behaves** → **product risk.**

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| | Project Risk | Product Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | Management and control | Product quality |
| **Categories** | Organizational, people, technical, supplier | Functional + non-functional defects |
| **Consequence** | Schedule/budget/scope deviation | Dissatisfaction, lost revenue, penalties, even death |
| **How to mitigate** | Planning, resources, communication | **Testing**, reviews, static analysis |
5.2.3:
## 1️⃣ What Is the Goal?

> From a testing perspective, the goal of **product risk analysis** is to **provide awareness of product risk** so that test effort is focused in a way that **minimizes the residual level of product risk**.

- ⏰ Ideally it begins **early in the SDLC**.

---

## 2️⃣ Two Steps

```
PRODUCT RISK ANALYSIS
    │
    ├── 1. RISK IDENTIFICATION
    │      → Generate a COMPREHENSIVE LIST of risks
    │      → Techniques: brainstorming, workshops,
    │                    interviews, cause-effect diagrams
    │
    └── 2. RISK ASSESSMENT
           → Categorize the identified risks
           → Determine likelihood + impact + risk level
           → Prioritize
           → Propose ways to handle them
```

- 🗂️ **Why categorize?** Risks in the same category can usually be mitigated with a **similar approach** → it makes assigning mitigation actions easier.

---

## 3️⃣ Quantitative or Qualitative?

| Approach | How the risk level is found | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 🔢 **Quantitative** | The **multiplication** of likelihood and impact | A number (e.g., 4 × 5 = 20) |
| 🎨 **Qualitative** | A **risk matrix** | Low / Medium / High |
| 🔀 **Mixed** | A blend of both | — |

---

## 4️⃣ What Are the Results Used For? (6 Items)

Product risk analysis influences the **thoroughness and scope** of testing. Its results are used to:

1. 📏 **Determine the test scope** to be carried out
2. 🧱 **Determine the particular test levels** and **propose the test types** to be performed
3. 🧰 Determine the **test techniques** to be employed and the **coverage** to be achieved
4. 🧮 **Estimate the test effort** required for each task
5. 🔢 **Prioritize testing** to find the **critical defects as early as possible**
6. 🛡️ Determine whether **activities in addition to testing** could reduce the risk

---

## 5️⃣ 💡 Concrete Example — Cloud Backup Tool

> **Analysis result:** "the restore function causes data loss" → **highest risk level**
> "the sort option in the backup list" → **low risk**

| Aspect | High-risk feature (restore) | Low-risk feature (sorting) |
|---|---|---|
| **Test depth** | Deep: boundary values, decision table, negative scenarios | Shallow: a few basic cases |
| **Test level/type** | Component + integration + system, reliability and recovery testing | Functional UI check only |
| **Coverage target** | High (e.g., 100% decision coverage) | Low |
| **Effort** | A lot | A little |
| **Order** | First | Last |
| **Extra activity** | Code review, static analysis, independent test team | None |

> 🔑 **High risk** → **deeper, broader, earlier** testing; **low risk** → **less** testing

---

| Step | What happens | Example technique/output |
|---|---|---|
| **Risk identification** | A comprehensive list of risks | Brainstorming, workshops, interviews, cause-effect diagrams |
| **Risk assessment** | Categorize, score, prioritize, propose handling | Quantitative product or a risk matrix |
| **Use of the results** | Scope, levels/types, techniques/coverage, effort, priority, extra activities | Test plan and test execution schedule |
5.2.4:
## 1️⃣ What Is Product Risk Control?

> **Product risk control** comprises **all the measures taken** in response to identified and assessed product risks.

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| 🛠️ **Risk mitigation** | **Implements the actions proposed** in risk assessment to reduce the risk level |
| 👁️ **Risk monitoring** | ① Ensures the mitigation actions are **effective** ② Obtains further information to **improve risk assessment** ③ **Identifies emerging risks** |

> 🔑 **Mitigation** → take the measure; **monitoring** → check whether the measure worked

---

## 2️⃣ Four Response Options to a Risk

| Option | What it means | When? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🧪 **Risk mitigation by testing** | Lower the risk by testing more/better | The risk lies in **how the software behaves** | Inefficient loop → **performance testing** |
| 🤝 **Risk acceptance** | Knowingly accept it, do nothing | You cannot control it, or control costs too much | **Consumers changing their preferences** |
| 📤 **Risk transfer** | Hand the risk to someone else (insurance, subcontractor) | External/environmental risks | **Flooding of the server room** → insurance |
| 🧯 **Contingency plan** | Write down in advance what to do if it happens | The impact is high | Failover plan to a backup data center |

*(Veenendaal 2012)*

---

## 3️⃣ 🧪 Mitigating Risk by Testing — 6 Actions

- 👤 **Select testers with the right level of experience and skills** for the given risk type
- 🔓 **Apply an appropriate level of independence of testing**
- 📖 **Perform reviews and static analysis**
- 🧰 **Apply the appropriate test techniques and coverage levels**
- 🎯 **Apply the appropriate test types** addressing the affected quality characteristics
- ▶️ **Perform dynamic testing, including regression testing**

---

## 4️⃣ 💡 Risk → Right Response (An Exam Classic)

| Risk | Best response |
|---|---|
| An inefficient loop implementation causes long system responses | 🧪 **Performance testing** |
| Consumers change their preferences | 🤝 **Risk acceptance** |
| The server room floods | 📤 **Risk transfer** (insurance) |
| Patients above a certain age receive incorrect reports | 🧪 Use **boundary value analysis** as the test technique |
| "The points calculation rule is implemented wrongly" (high risk) | 🧪 **Deep functional testing with decision tables/boundary values** + **code review / static analysis** |

> 💡 **Worked example — a risk register row:**
> ```
> Risk        : Response time for report generation is too long
> Likelihood  : Medium    Impact: High    → Risk level: High
> Handling    : • An independent test team performs PERFORMANCE TESTING in system testing
>               • A sample of end users performs ALPHA and BETA ACCEPTANCE TESTING before release
> → This is an example of RISK MITIGATION (by testing)
> ```

---

| Concept | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Product risk control** | All measures taken against identified risks |
| **Risk mitigation** | Implement the proposed actions → bring the risk level down |
| **Risk monitoring** | Did the measure work? Are there new risks? |
| **Response options** | Mitigation by testing · Acceptance · Transfer · Contingency plan |
5.3:
## 1️⃣ Three Activities, Three Questions

| Activity | Its question | In short |
|---|---|---|
| 👁️ **Test monitoring** | "What is the status?" | **Gathers information** about testing |
| 🎮 **Test control** | "What should we do?" | Turns that information into **corrective action** |
| ✅ **Test completion** | "What did we learn, what do we archive?" | **Collects and consolidates** experience and testware |

> 🔑 **Monitoring** measures → **control** intervenes → **completion** closes

---

## 2️⃣ 👁️ Test Monitoring

The gathered information is used to:
- 📈 **Assess test progress**
- 🚦 **Measure whether the exit criteria** (or the test tasks associated with them) **are satisfied** — e.g., meeting the targets for **coverage of product risks, requirements or acceptance criteria**

---

## 3️⃣ 🎮 Test Control — Control Directives

Test control turns monitoring information into guidance and **corrective actions**, in the form of **control directives**. Examples:

- 🔁 **Reprioritizing tests when an identified risk becomes an issue**
- 🚦 **Re-evaluating whether a test item meets entry or exit criteria** due to rework
- 📅 **Adjusting the test schedule** to address a **delay in the delivery of the test environment**
- ➕ **Adding new resources** when and where needed

> 💡 Example — e-commerce cart: the plan said 50 cases a week, 30 were run. Cause: the test environment crashed → **control directive:** fix the environment, update the schedule, add one more tester.

---

## 4️⃣ ✅ Test Completion

It **collects data from completed test activities to consolidate** experience, testware and any other relevant information.

### When does it happen? → **At project milestones**
- When a **test level** is completed
- When an **Agile iteration** is finished
- When a **test project** is completed **(or cancelled)**
- When a **software system is released**
- When a **maintenance release** is completed

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| | Monitoring | Control | Completion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What it does** | Gathers information/metrics | Issues corrective action | Consolidates experience and testware |
| **Output** | Test progress report, metrics | **Control directives** | **Test completion report**, archive, lessons learned |
| **When** | Continuously | Whenever there is a deviation | At milestones |

## 1️⃣ Why Are Metrics Gathered?

Test metrics are gathered to show:
- 📅 **Progress against the planned test schedule and budget**
- 💎 The **current quality of the test object**
- 🎯 The **effectiveness of test activities** with respect to the test objectives or an iteration goal

> **Test monitoring** gathers the metrics → they support **test control** and **test completion**.

---

## 2️⃣ Seven Metric Categories

| # | Category | Examples | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 📋 **Project progress metrics** | Task completion, **resource usage**, **test effort** | Where we stand against the project plan |
| 2 | 🧪 **Test progress metrics** | Test case **implementation progress**, **test environment preparation progress**, number of test cases **run/not run**, **passed/failed**, **test execution time** | How far the testing work has got |
| 3 | 💎 **Product quality metrics** | **Availability**, **response time**, **mean time to failure** | **How good the product is** |
| 4 | 🐛 **Defect metrics** | **Number and priorities** of defects found/fixed, **defect density**, **defect detection percentage** | How many defects, how dense |
| 5 | ⚠️ **Risk metrics** | **Residual risk level** | How much risk is still there |
| 6 | 📐 **Coverage metrics** | **Requirements coverage**, **code coverage** | How much we have covered |
| 7 | 💰 **Cost metrics** | **Cost of testing**, **organizational cost of quality** | What it cost |

---

| Metric | Category |
|---|---|
| Number of test cases executed | 🧪 **Test progress** |
| Number of test cases passed/remaining | 🧪 **Test progress** |
| Test environment readiness % | 🧪 **Test progress** |
| **Response time** | 💎 **Product quality** |
| **Availability (uptime)** | 💎 **Product quality** |
| **Mean time to failure** | 💎 **Product quality** |
| **Requirements coverage %** | 📐 **Coverage** |
| **Code coverage %** | 📐 **Coverage** |
| Defect density | 🐛 **Defect** |

| Test effort spent | 📋 **Project progress** |

> 🔑 **"How is the product behaving?"** → a product quality metric
> 🔑 **"Where is the test team?"** → a test progress metric

5.3.2:
## 1️⃣ What Does a Test Report Do?

> Test reporting **summarizes and communicates test information during and after testing.**

There are two kinds, and **the exam expects you to mix them up:**

| | 📊 **Test Progress Report** (status report) | 🏁 **Test Completion Report** |
|---|---|---|
| **When?** | **Regularly** (daily, weekly) — **while** testing runs | **Once**, during **test completion** |
| **What it supports** | **Ongoing test control** | Giving information for subsequent testing |
| **Which activity uses it** | **Test monitoring and control** | **Test completion** |
| **Scope** | That **testing period** | The completed **project / test level / test type** |
| **Formality** | Within the same team usually **frequent and informal** | **Follows a set template** |
| **Precondition** | None | **Ideally the exit criteria have been met** |

> 🔑 **Progress report** → "where are we now, what should we change?"
> 🔑 **Completion report** → "what happened, what is left, what did we learn?"

---

## 2️⃣ 📊 Test Progress Report Content

- 📅 **Testing period**
- 📈 **Test progress** (ahead of or behind schedule) — including **any notable deviations**
- 🚧 **Impediments for testing, and their workarounds**
- 📊 **Test metrics** (see 5.3.1)
- ⚠️ **New and changed risks** within the testing period
- ⏭️ **Testing planned for the next period**

> ⚠️ A progress report must provide **enough information to modify the test schedule, resources or test plan** when changes are needed because of deviation from the plan or changed circumstances.

---

## 3️⃣ 🏁 Test Completion Report Content

- 📝 **Test summary**
- 💎 **Testing and product quality evaluation based on the original test plan** (test objectives and exit criteria)
- ↔️ **Deviations from the test plan** (differences from the planned schedule, duration and effort)
- 🚧 **Testing impediments and workarounds**
- 📊 **Test metrics based on the test progress reports**
- ⚠️ **Unmitigated risks, defects not fixed**
- 💡 **Lessons learned relevant to the testing**

---

## 4️⃣ 🎯 The Audience Changes Everything

- Different audiences need **different information**
- The audience influences the **degree of formality and the frequency** of reporting
- Progress reporting to others in the same team: **frequent and informal**
- Completion reporting: a **set template**, **only once**

> 📚 **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3** contains **templates and examples** for test progress reports (also called **test status reports**) and test completion reports.

---

## ❌ These Are NOT Valid Purposes of a Test Report
- ❌ **Finding and fixing the root cause** of a defect → that is debugging
- ❌ **Appraising or blaming developers** on their performance
- ❌ **Writing code or doing design**
- ❌ Giving the **step-by-step design of test cases** → that is an output of test design

## 1️⃣ There Is No Single Right Way

The best means of communicating test status **varies** with:
- 🧭 **Test management concerns**
- 🏢 **Organizational test strategies**
- ⚖️ **Regulatory standards**
- 👥 **In self-organizing teams → the team itself**

---

## 2️⃣ Five Communication Options

| Option | Example | Formality |
|---|---|---|
| 🗣️ **Verbal communication** | Talking to team members and stakeholders, the daily stand-up | Lowest |
| 📊 **Dashboards** | **CI/CD dashboards**, **task boards**, **burn-down charts** | Low–medium |
| 💬 **Electronic communication channels** | Email, chat | Medium |
| 📄 **Online documentation** | A Confluence page, a wiki | Medium–high |
| 📑 **Formal test reports** | Test progress and test completion reports (see 5.3.2) | Highest |

> **One or more** of these options can be used together.

---

## 3️⃣ Two Golden Rules

### 🌍 1. Distributed teams need more formal communication
> When **direct face-to-face communication is not always possible** because of geographical distance or time differences → **more formal communication is more appropriate.**

> 💡 Example: the team is in North America, the customer in Europe → **verbal/instant chat is the least effective way**; a CI/CD dashboard plus a written report is the right choice.

### 🎯 2. Each stakeholder gets their own information
> Different stakeholders are interested in **different types of information** → **communication should be tailored accordingly.**

| Stakeholder | What they care about | Suitable channel |
|---|---|---|
| 👨‍💻 **Developers (daily)** | Which test failed, defect detail | **CI/CD dashboard**, chat, daily stand-up |
| 📦 **Product owner** | Are the stories done, are acceptance criteria met | **Task board, burn-down chart**, iteration demo |
| 👔 **Senior management** | Risk, quality, the release decision | **Formal test progress/completion report** |

## 4️⃣ 📉 The Burn-Down Chart

> The work product used to show **how much work an Agile team has completed in a given iteration (sprint) and how much total work remains** = the **burn-down chart**.

```
Work    ▲
remain. │╲
        │ ╲___
        │     ╲╲
        │       ╲╲___
        └──────────────▶ Days in the iteration
```

| DevOps / CI-CD pipeline | **CI/CD dashboard** |

5.4:
## 1️⃣ What Is Configuration Management?

> In testing, **configuration management (CM)** provides a **discipline** for **identifying, controlling and tracking** work products as **configuration items**.

### Which work products become configuration items?
- 📄 **Test plans**, 🧭 **test strategies**
- ✅ **Test conditions**, 📝 **test cases**, 🤖 **test scripts**
- 📊 **Test results**, 📒 **test logs**, 📑 **test reports**

> 💡 For a **complex configuration item** (e.g., a **test environment**), CM records **the items it consists of, their relationships and their versions**.

---

## 2️⃣ The Baseline Logic

```
A configuration item is APPROVED for testing
        ↓
It becomes a BASELINE
        ↓
From then on it can only change through a FORMAL CHANGE CONTROL PROCESS
        ↓
When a new baseline is created → a RECORD OF CHANGED ITEMS is kept
        ↓
It is possible to REVERT TO A PREVIOUS BASELINE
        ↓
→ PREVIOUS TEST RESULTS CAN BE REPRODUCED ✅
```

---

## 3️⃣ How Does CM Support Testing? (2 Guarantees)

| Guarantee | What it means |
|---|---|
| 🔖 **Unique identity + versions + traceability** | **All configuration items**, including test items, are **uniquely identified**, **version controlled**, **tracked for changes** and **related to one another** → **traceability is maintained** throughout the test process |
| 🔗 **No ambiguity** | All identified **documentation and software items** are **referenced unambiguously** in the testware |

---

## 4️⃣ 💡 Real Life — A Video Conference Recording Service Releasing Twice a Week

| Need | CM's answer |
|---|---|
| "Which release did this failure appear in?" | Every build is tagged with a **unique version number** |
| "Which test cases tested that release?" | Test cases are **versioned configuration items** too, and **related** to the release |
| "Can we reproduce the defect?" | **Revert to the previous baseline** → same environment, same data, same result |
| "The user gave us a version number — can we rebuild it?" | CM lets the team **reassemble all the components** that made that release → the developer analyses and fixes |
| "I updated the test script — how is that recorded?" | **Checking in / committing the script to the test repository as a new version** |

---

## 5️⃣ Its Relationship with DevOps

> **Continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous deployment** and the associated testing are typically implemented as part of an automated **DevOps pipeline** — and **automated CM is normally included in it.**

---

## ❌ These Are NOT Examples of CM Supporting Testing
- ❌ Assigning a **severity** to a defect report → defect management
- ❌ **Designing** test cases → test design
- ❌ **Calculating a risk level** → risk analysis
- ❌ **Estimating effort** → test planning

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Concept | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Configuration item** | Any work product that is versioned and tracked (plan, case, script, log, report, environment) |
| **Baseline** | The state approved for testing, changeable only through a formal process |
| **Change control** | The only formal way to change a baseline |
| **Reverting** | Going back to a previous baseline to **reproduce previous test results** |
| **Traceability** | Which test covers which version and which requirement — all linked |

> 🔑 **Without CM** there is no answer to "which release was this defect found in, and with which test?"
5.5:
## 1️⃣ Why Is Defect Management Essential?

Since one of the major test objectives is to **find defects**, an **established defect management process** is essential.

> ⚠️ Although we say "defect", a **reported anomaly** may turn out to be something else:
> - ✅ A real **defect**
> - ❌ A **false-positive result** → the test was wrong, the software was right
> - 🔄 A **change request** → not a defect, a new wish
>
> Which one it is **gets resolved during the process of dealing with the defect reports.**

Anomalies may be reported **during any phase of the SDLC**, and **the form depends on the SDLC**.

---

## 2️⃣ The Defect Management Process — The Minimum

At a minimum the process includes:
- 🔁 A **workflow** for handling individual defects or anomalies **from discovery to closure**
- 🗂️ **Rules for their classification**

```
ANOMALY IS DISCOVERED
    ↓
LOG it
    ↓
ANALYZE and CLASSIFY it
    ↓
DECIDE ON A SUITABLE RESPONSE → fix / keep as is / reject
    ↓
CLOSE the defect report
```

- 👥 The process **must be followed by all involved stakeholders.**
- 📖 It is **advisable to handle defects from static testing** (especially **static analysis**) **in a similar way.**

---

## 3️⃣ The 3 Objectives of a Defect Report

1. 🛠️ Provide those **responsible for handling and resolving** reported defects with **sufficient information to resolve the issue**
2. 📊 Provide a means of **tracking the quality of the work product**
3. 💡 Provide **ideas for improvement of the development and test process**

---

## 4️⃣ 📋 What Must Be In a Defect Report? (The Checklist)

| # | Field | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 🆔 **Unique identifier** | DEF-114 |
| 2 | 🏷️ **Title with a short summary** | "Total application score is calculated incorrectly" |
| 3 | 📅 **Date observed, issuing organization, author (including their role)** | 2026-03-12, Test Team, A. Demir (tester) |
| 4 | 🖥️ **Identification of the test object and test environment** | Portal v3.2, ENV-2, Chrome 126 |
| 5 | 🧩 **Context of the defect** | Test case being run, test activity, SDLC phase, test technique, checklist, test data used |
| 6 | 🔁 **Description of the failure + steps to reproduce** | Steps + relevant **test logs, database dumps, screenshots or recordings** |
| 7 | ⚖️ **Expected results and actual results** | Expected: 85 points / Actual: 78 points |
| 8 | 💥 **Severity** | The **degree of impact** on the interests of stakeholders or requirements |
| 9 | 🔢 **Priority to fix** | High / Medium / Low |
| 10 | 🚦 **Status of the defect** | Open, deferred, **duplicate**, waiting to be fixed, **awaiting confirmation testing**, re-opened, closed, **rejected** |
| 11 | 🔗 **References** | The related test case, requirement |

> 🤖 With a defect management tool some data is filled in **automatically**: **identifier, date, author and initial status**.
> 📚 Templates and examples: **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3** — that standard calls defect reports **incident reports**.

---

## 5️⃣ ⚠️ Severity ≠ Priority

| | **Severity** | **Priority** |
|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | The **size of the technical/business impact** | **How urgently it must be fixed** |
| **Who sets it** | Usually the tester | Usually the product owner / management |
| **Example** | A crash in a rarely used report → **high severity, low priority** | A typo on the home page → **low severity, high priority** |

---

## 6️⃣ 🔎 How to Spot an Incomplete Defect Report

> 💡 **Example — an incomplete report:**
> ```
> Application: WebShop v0.99
> Defect: The login button does not work
> Steps: Launch the website → click the login button
> Expected: The user should be taken to the login page
> Actual: The login button does not respond
> ```
> ❌ **Missing:** identification of the test environment (browser/OS), date and author, severity/priority, status, unique identifier, screenshot.
> → The developer cannot tell **which environment** to try → the defect **cannot be reproduced**.

> 💡 **A report rejected as "not reproducible"** usually lacks a clear **test environment, test data or steps**.

---

## 🧠 Summary Table

| Question | Its answer in the defect report |
|---|---|
| Which defect? | Unique identifier + title |
| Who found it, when? | Date, organization, author + role |
| Where did it happen? | Test object + test environment |
| Under what conditions? | Context of the defect (case, technique, data) |
| How do I reproduce it? | Steps to reproduce + logs/screenshots |
| What should have happened vs what did? | Expected vs actual results |
| How bad is it? | Severity |
| How urgent is it? | Priority |
| Where does it stand now? | Status |
| What is it linked to? | References |

> 🔑 **A good defect report** = the developer can reproduce the defect **without asking a single question**
6.1:
## 1️⃣ What Does a Tool Actually Do?

Test tools do not **think for you** — they make testing **faster, easier and measurable**. Every test activity has its own family of tools.

> 🔑 Tool → **support**, decision → **human**

---

## 2️⃣ Tool Categories (the ISTQB List)

| Category | What it does | Real example tool |
|---|---|---|
| 📋 **Test Management Tools** | Manage the SDLC, requirements, tests, **defects** and **configuration** → raise process efficiency | Jira, TestRail, Azure DevOps Boards |
| 🔍 **Static Testing Tools** | Support reviews and analyse code **without running it** | SonarQube, ESLint, Checkstyle |
| ✏️ **Test Design and Implementation Tools** | Generate test cases, **test data** and test procedures | Mockaroo, Faker, data generators |
| ▶️ **Test Execution and Coverage Tools** | **Run tests automatically** + measure **which lines/branches ran** | Selenium, JUnit, JaCoCo, Cobertura |
| ⚡ **Non-Functional Testing Tools** | Tests that are **hard or impossible** by hand: load, performance, security | JMeter, k6, OWASP ZAP |
| 🔁 **DevOps Tools** | Delivery pipeline, **workflow tracking**, automated builds, **CI/CD** | Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions |
| 🗣️ **Collaboration Tools** | Make **communication** easier | Slack, Microsoft Teams, Confluence |
| 📦 **Scalability and Deployment Standardization** | **Virtual machines**, containers → every environment identical | Docker, Kubernetes, VMware |
| 🧰 **Any other tool that assists testing** | **Anything** used in the context of testing | A spreadsheet is a test tool too! |

> 🔑 Even a **spreadsheet** counts as a **test tool** when it is used in a testing context

---

## 3️⃣ The Exam Distinction: Which Phrase Means Which Category?

| Phrase in the question | Correct category |
|---|---|
| "Scans the source **without executing it**, reports unused variables / unreachable code / standard violations" | 🔍 **Static testing tools** |
| "Measure **which lines / which branches** were executed" | ▶️ **Test execution and coverage tools** |
| "A **test data** preparation tool" | ✏️ **Test design and implementation tools** |
| "Organise test cases + defects + **configuration management**" | 📋 **Test management tools** |
| "**Workflow tracking**, automated builds, CI/CD" | 🔁 **DevOps tools** |
| "Facilitating **communication**" | 🗣️ **Collaboration tools** |
| "**Virtual machines**, containers" | 📦 **Scalability tools** |
| "Supporting **reviews**" | 🔍 **Static testing tools** |
| "Simulate 5,000 concurrent users under **load**" | ⚡ **Non-functional testing tools** |

## ⚠️ The Favourite Trap: Nightly Suite + Coverage

The question looks like this: *"After every nightly build the regression suite should run automatically and we want to measure which lines of code were executed."*

```
"Runs automatically every night"   → sounds like DevOps
"Which lines were executed"        → but COVERAGE measurement decides it
        ↓
Answer: Test Execution and Coverage Tools ✅
```

> 🔑 If the question mentions **coverage measurement**, the answer is **not DevOps** — it is **execution and coverage** tools

## 4️⃣ Who Actually Runs the Tests?

### ✅ These directly facilitate **executing** tests:
- 🔁 **DevOps tools** → the CI/CD pipeline triggers and runs the tests
- ⚡ **Non-functional testing tools** → actually perform the load/performance test
- ▶️ **Test execution tools** → run the scripts

### ❌ These do **not** run tests, they prepare for them:
- 📋 **Management tools** → plan and track
- 🗣️ **Collaboration tools** → keep people talking
- ✏️ **Design tools** → produce cases and data

- ❌ Think critically and make risk decisions
- ❌ Fix a bad test process on their own
- ❌ Prove "there are no defects"
- ❌ Pay off the moment you buy them → **introduction, maintenance and training** effort is mandatory

## 1️⃣ The Golden Rule First

Simply **acquiring** a tool does not guarantee good testing. Every new tool demands effort before it delivers real and lasting benefits:

- 🔧 **Tool introduction**
- 🛠️ **Maintenance**
- 📚 **Training**

> 🔑 Tool → **possibility**, effort → **benefit**. No effort, no benefit.

---

## 2️⃣ Benefits

| Benefit | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ⏰ **Time saved** | Less repetitive manual work | 400 regression tests run themselves at 3 a.m. |
| ✅ **Consistency and repeatability** | Simple human errors are prevented | Test data is generated systematically, tests run in the same order every time |
| 📊 **More objective assessment** | Measures too complicated for humans | **Coverage** percentage: "73% of branches executed" |
| 📈 **Easier access to information** | Feeds test management and reporting | Statistics, graphs, failure rates, execution duration |
| 🚀 **Reduced execution time** | **Earlier** defect detection, faster feedback, faster time to market | "You broke it" eight minutes after the commit |
| 🧠 **More time for testers** | They design new, deeper, more effective tests | Clicking goes to the machine, exploratory testing stays with the human |

---

## 3️⃣ Risks

| Risk | What it means | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|
| 🎭 **Unrealistic expectations** | The tool's functionality and ease of use are oversold | "Once this is in, manual testing is over" |
| 💸 **Inaccurate estimations** | Introduction, script **maintenance** and changing the manual process are underestimated | A two-week job stretches to four months |
| 🖐️ **Using a tool where manual is more appropriate** | Automating one-off or exploratory testing | Three days of scripting for a test that runs once |
| 🤖 **Relying on a tool too much** | Ignoring the need for human **critical thinking** | "The suite is green, so the product is fine" |
| 🏢 **Vendor dependency** | The vendor may go out of business, retire or sell the tool, or give poor support | No answers to queries, defect fixes never ship |
| 🧟 **Abandoned open-source** | No further updates, or internal components need constant updating | No commits for three years, broken on the new browser |
| 🔌 **Platform incompatibility** | The tool does not work with the development platform | An automation tool that does not support your mobile framework |
| ⚖️ **Unsuitable tool choice** | Does not comply with regulatory requirements or safety standards | No traceability in a medical device project |

---

## 4️⃣ How These Risks Actually Show Up

| What you see day to day | The official risk behind it |
|---|---|
| 🎲 **Flaky tests** — same code, passes one run, fails the next | Inaccurate estimation of maintenance effort + over-reliance |
| 🧱 One small UI change breaks 200 scripts | Underestimated script **maintenance** cost |
| 😴 The team ignores red builds because "it's always red" | Over-reliance → critical thinking is gone |
| 🚫 No exploratory testing, because "everything is automated" | Using a tool where manual testing is more appropriate |
| 🕸️ Stuck on an old version, unable to upgrade | Abandoned open-source / vendor dependency |

> 🔑 A flaky test is not a tool defect, it is **maintenance debt** → unmaintained automation becomes untrusted automation

## 5️⃣ Exam Traps: Benefit or Risk?

### ✅ These are **benefits**:
- Less repetitive work
- Consistency and repeatability
- Objective coverage measurement
- Easy access to reporting data
- Earlier defect detection and faster feedback
- More tester time for test design

### ❌ These are **not** benefits:
- "Automation finds **more** defects" → ❌ Not **more**, but **earlier**
- "Automation makes manual testing unnecessary" → ❌ That is a **risk**
- "Automation cuts cost immediately" → ❌ Introduction, training and maintenance costs **rise** first
- "A tool replaces critical thinking" → ❌ That is exactly the **over-reliance risk**
- "A tool fixes a bad test process" → ❌ Automate a bad process and it is just bad **faster**
